meta.name: AST SpaceMobile, Inc.
meta.title: AST SpaceMobile — Abel Avellan's direct-to-cell satellite network through the BlueBird constellation
meta.subtitle: From the 2017 Midland-Texas founding through the 2021 SPAC listing into the BlueBird operational deployment that targets satellite-to-standard-smartphone connectivity at global scale
meta.abstract: AST SpaceMobile, Inc. (ASTS, NASDAQ) is the Midland, Texas-headquartered direct-to-cell satellite operator developing the SpaceMobile network — a low Earth orbit satellite constellation designed to provide cellular broadband service directly to standard unmodified mobile phones in partnership with terrestrial mobile network operators globally. The company was founded in 2017 by Abel Avellan, the Venezuelan-born telecommunications and satellite industry executive who previously founded Emerging Markets Communications and held senior roles at Hughes Electronics and Astrolink. AST SpaceMobile went public via SPAC business combination with New Providence Acquisition Corp in April 2021. Avellan continues as Chairman of the Board and CEO; CFO Andrew Johnson, Chief Strategy Officer Sean Wallace, and the broader executive team support the multi-year capital-intensive constellation deployment programme. The strategic differentiation is structural — AST SpaceMobile is one of only two meaningful commercial direct-to-cell satellite operators (the other being SpaceX Starlink's emerging direct-to-cell service through partnership with T-Mobile). The five operational BlueBird satellites launched in September 2024 demonstrated the direct-to-cell capability at commercial scale; subsequent Block 2 BlueBird satellites at substantially larger antenna scale (approximately 64 square metres of phased array antenna per satellite) are intended to deploy through 2026-2027 to establish broader commercial coverage. The mobile network operator partnership base includes AT&T (US), Verizon (US), Vodafone (multi-country), Rakuten (Japan), Bell Canada, Telefonica (multi-country), and Orange (multi-country) — covering an addressable subscriber base in the billions globally. Fiscal year 2025 (calendar year 2025) revenue was minimal as the company remains substantially pre-commercial; the FY2025 net loss was substantial reflecting the constellation deployment capex plus broader R&D investment. The cash position at year-end 2025 was substantial reflecting multiple equity issuances supporting the multi-year deployment. The investment proposition compresses the constellation deployment execution timeline, the commercial revenue scaling once Block 2 satellites reach operational coverage, the mobile network operator partnership monetisation, and the competitive dynamics versus SpaceX Starlink's direct-to-cell service plus emerging satellite-to-handset alternatives.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
On 12 September 2024, a SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off from Cape Canaveral carrying five BlueBird satellites, the first operational nodes of AST SpaceMobile's direct-to-cell network. The launch marked the end of the company's prototype phase and the beginning of an early operational one for AST SpaceMobile (ASTS, Nasdaq), whose premise had been that a low-Earth-orbit constellation with very large phased-array antennas could connect ordinary, unmodified smartphones through mobile operators' existing spectrum rather than through specialist satellite handsets or a bespoke spectrum layer. By the time of the frozen snapshot, management said the commercial partner base had expanded to nearly 60 mobile network operators covering more than 3 billion subscribers, including AT&T, Bell Canada, MTN, Orange, Rakuten, Verizon, Vodafone and others. [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

## The Architecture of the Founding Thesis

AST SpaceMobile's proposition to operators was structurally different from earlier satellite-phone ventures. The satellite was meant to behave as a roaming cell tower in orbit, handing traffic back into terrestrial networks and using the licensed frequencies of partner mobile network operators. The physics problem was severe: consumer handsets transmit with limited power, so the space segment had to supply the antenna gain. BlueWalker 3, the prototype launched on 10 September 2022, carried a 693-square-foot phased array and became the vehicle through which AST demonstrated the world's first voice call, video call and 5G connection from space to everyday smartphones. By May 2026 the company was also pointing to the FCC's grant of Supplemental Coverage from Space authority in the United States as a regulatory milestone that moved the concept from testing into authorized commercial service. [BlueWalker 3](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluewalker-3/); [first voice call](https://ast-science.com/2023/04/25/ast-spacemobile-makes-history-in-cellular-connectivity-completing-the-first-ever-space-based-voice-call-using-everyday-unmodified-smartphones/); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

The company reached public markets on 7 April 2021, when it completed its business combination with New Providence Acquisition Corp and began trading as ASTS. The listing supplied public-company currency, but the years that followed were spent on the harder tasks: moving from the BlueWalker 3 proof satellite to production hardware, building Midland manufacturing capacity, signing definitive commercial agreements, and navigating the still-forming regulatory framework for supplemental coverage from space. [ASTS listing announcement](https://ast-science.com/2021/04/06/nasdaq-asts/)

## BlueBird Constellation: Block 1 and the First Block 2 Node

The five BlueBird Block 1 satellites launched in September 2024 were the first commercial satellites in the series. According to AST's own product pages, they carried 693-square-foot arrays, 40 MHz of bandwidth and peak transmission speeds of 120 Mbps per coverage cell, with about 95% vertical integration across the company's Midland-area assembly, integration and testing facilities. The company had already shifted the production emphasis to its next-generation Block 2 design, which it described as roughly three times larger than Block 1 with about 10 times the data capacity. [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/); [How it works](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/our-technology/); [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/)

The first Block 2 unit, BlueBird 6, launched on 23 December 2025 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in India. AST described it as carrying a phased array of nearly 2,400 square feet, again the largest commercial communications array it had deployed in low Earth orbit. The second Block 2 unit, BlueBird 7, launched on Blue Origin's New Glenn on 19 April 2026, but AST told investors that the upper stage placed the satellite into a lower-than-planned orbit, too low to sustain operations with its onboard thruster technology. The company deorbited the spacecraft, said it expected a replacement launch under its contract with the launch provider, and estimated the carrying value of the lost satellite at $155 million to $160 million, to be written off in the second quarter of 2026. [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/); [BlueBird 7 launch update](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315226018012/ex99-1.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

## Revenue, Capital, and the MNO Partnership Stack

Revenue through the frozen window remained pre-mass-market. AST reported $70.9 million of revenue for full-year 2025 and $14.7 million for the first quarter of 2026. Management said the 2025 figure had been driven by mobile network operator partners and the U.S. government, while the first-quarter 2026 figure was driven by gateway deliveries and government milestones. As of 31 March 2026 the company also disclosed roughly $1.2 billion of remaining performance obligations, alongside the Verizon $45 million contingent prepaid-service commitment and the 10-year stc agreement that included a $175 million prepayment commitment during 2025. [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm); [stc 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315225020005/form8-k.htm)

The capital structure reflected the demands of a multi-year satellite build-out. In January 2024 AST announced strategic investments and commercial commitments from AT&T, Google and Vodafone that, together with related capital actions, were described as worth up to $306.5 million in gross proceeds; in May 2024 Verizon added a $100 million financial commitment made up of $65 million of commercial prepayments and $35 million of convertible notes. After Block 1, AST leaned more heavily on convertible debt: $460 million of 4.25% notes issued in January 2025, $575 million of 2.375% notes in July 2025, $1.15 billion of 2.00% notes in October 2025, and $1.075 billion of 2.25% notes in February 2026 including the exercised option for additional notes. As of 31 March 2026, the 10-Q showed $3.46 billion of cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash, including about $429 million of restricted cash. [January 2024 strategic investment 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224002914/form8-k.htm); [Verizon 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224021726/form8-k.htm); [January 2025 notes](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315225003793/ex99-1.htm); [July 2025 notes 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225021421/form8-k.htm); [2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000006/asts-20251231.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

## The Competitive Frame

The commercial reference point by the frozen snapshot was no longer hypothetical. T-Mobile said in July 2025 that T-Satellite would launch nationwide on 23 July with SMS for iOS and Android, MMS and picture messaging, and short audio clips for Android, and that more than 657 Starlink direct-to-cell satellites were already in orbit. SpaceX's own updates traced the system back to January 2024, when it said it had sent first text messages using T-Mobile spectrum through newly launched direct-to-cell satellites. In April 2026 the FCC separately approved an additional 7,500 Gen2 satellites for direct-to-cell operations outside the United States and supplemental coverage from space. Against that backdrop, AST's own filings said it expected noncontinuous service in targeted markets with 25 total BlueBird satellites, continuous coverage across key markets such as the United States, Europe and Japan with approximately 45 to 60 satellites, and continuous service across all targeted geographies with approximately 90 satellites. [T-Mobile July 2025 launch](https://www.t-mobile.com/news/network/best-network-in-america); [T-Satellite available](https://www.t-mobile.com/news/network/t-satellite-now-available); [Starlink first-text update](https://starlink.com/public-files/DIRECT_TO_CELL_FIRST_TEXT_UPDATE.pdf); [FCC DA-26-36A1](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.pdf); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

---

From that posture, the core questions were not abstract. They were whether Block 2 production and launch cadence could reach the 25-satellite and then 45-to-60-satellite thresholds on schedule; whether nearly 60 mobile-network agreements could convert into recurring usage revenue once coverage became continuous enough to matter; how quickly Starlink's commercial head start could harden into operator and consumer habit; and whether AST's liquidity and restricted-cash structure were enough to finance the constellation through the point where the network began funding itself. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: From 2017 founding through BlueWalker 3, SPAC, and BlueBird operational launches
chapters.body:
## Midland Origins: The Founding Thesis

Abel Avellan founded AST & Science in Midland, Texas in May 2017 after selling Emerging Markets Communications, the satellite-services company he had built, for $550 million in July 2016. The corporate materials consistently described the new venture as a bet that ordinary handsets were already radio-compatible with a sufficiently large, space-based phased array, and that the commercial opportunity lay in extending terrestrial mobile networks into the vast share of the planet that remained outside tower coverage. By the time of AST's current disclosures, the company's public materials were citing more than 87% of the Earth's surface as outside the reach of traditional cellular networks. [Board bio](https://ast-science.com/investors/governance/board-of-directors/); [Cisneros investment release](https://ast-science.com/cisneros-investment/); [FAQ](https://ast-science.com/faqs/)

He established AST SpaceMobile in Midland, Texas — an energy-industry town whose infrastructure and landlord economics suited an early-stage hardware business better than the coastal aerospace corridors around Los Angeles or northern Virginia. The founding thesis was precise: engineer a low Earth orbit satellite carrying a phased-array antenna large enough to communicate directly with standard, unmodified smartphones on the cellular spectrum bands that mobile network operators already licensed and their customers already used. No special handset. No proprietary terminal. The service would arrive over existing LTE and eventually 5G NR air interfaces, delivered from orbit at roughly 500 kilometres altitude, and sold to consumers through the MNO partner rather than directly. The satellite network would function as a seamless extension of the terrestrial mobile network — invisible infrastructure extending coverage into the roughly 85 percent of the Earth's surface that ground-based towers did not reach.

The engineering challenge embedded in that thesis was formidable. Communicating directly with a handset from LEO required concentrating enough signal through an antenna surface area orders of magnitude larger than any satellite the industry had previously attempted in that orbit. Avellan's engineering team set to work on a foldable phased-array design that could be stowed inside a rocket fairing and then unfurl in orbit to dimensions previously associated with large GEO communications platforms rather than nimble LEO craft. The technical credibility of the approach — or the lack of it — would define how much capital the company could attract before flight hardware validated the physics.

## Early Capital and the MNO Partnership Architecture

The first strategic capital arrived before AST had public-market access. On 3 March 2020 the company announced that Rakuten and Vodafone had become lead investors in the effort to build a space-based mobile broadband network, turning the early cap table into the first expression of the MNO-partnership model that would later define the business. The commercial architecture was explicit: AST would not try to own the subscriber. It would supply the space segment, the operator would contribute licensed spectrum and customer billing, and the economics would be built around revenue share, prepaid commitments and related commercial arrangements rather than a conventional wholesale-capacity lease. [Rakuten and Vodafone investment](https://ast-science.com/2020/03/03/rakuten-vodafone-invest-in-ast/); [2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000006/asts-20251231.htm)

The partnership model that crystallised from those early relationships established the commercial template the company would carry through listing and into operations. Rather than licensing spectrum independently or selling handsets, AST would operate the satellite network on behalf of MNO partners, which would retain the subscriber relationship and billing infrastructure. Early revenue did not come from consumer satellite service. The 2022 10-K showed $13.8 million of revenue from the legacy NanoAvionika subsidiary; after AST sold its 51% stake in Nano in September 2022, 2023 revenue fell to zero before later government and gateway revenue began to appear. [2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017023011124/asts-20221231.htm); [2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024039342/asts-20231231.htm)

AT&T later signed AST's definitive U.S. commercial agreement in May 2024, and Verizon entered first through a May 2024 memorandum backed by prepayments and convertible financing, then through a definitive commercial agreement in October 2025. Bell Canada, Telstra, MTN and other operators broadened the roster internationally, and by May 2026 AST was describing nearly 60 mobile network operator relationships covering more than 3 billion subscribers. Google joined the January 2024 strategic investment round alongside AT&T and Vodafone, adding technology-sector endorsement to a company still scaling toward commercial coverage. [AT&T Commercial Agreement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024097099/asts-20240630.htm); [Verizon 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224021726/form8-k.htm); [January 2024 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224002914/form8-k.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

## The April 2021 SPAC Merger

Public-market capital arrived on 7 April 2021, when AST completed its merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp and began trading on Nasdaq as ASTS. The transaction gave the company listed equity currency, but it did not remove the two central execution dependencies: first, proving that direct-to-cell physics worked in orbit; second, finding enough capital to manufacture and launch satellites in meaningful numbers once that proof existed. [ASTS listing announcement](https://ast-science.com/2021/04/06/nasdaq-asts/)

The listing placed the founding thesis, and its execution risks, squarely in front of public investors. The company was pre-revenue in any commercial sense, carried significant operating losses, and still needed both on-orbit proof and a much larger capital base before a commercial network could exist. By the 2025 proxy, the stockholders' agreement gave Avellan extensive nomination rights, while Vodafone, American Tower, AT&T and Antares each had their own designation rights and Rakuten retained board-seat and observer rights subject to ownership thresholds. That governance picture was more precise than the earlier shorthand around a single founder-run structure: by the frozen window Avellan was chairman and chief executive officer, while Scott Wisniewski served as president and chief strategy officer. [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225006182/formdef14a.htm); [Management team](https://ast-science.com/investors/governance/management-team/)

## BlueWalker 3: Proof of Physics

The first decisive technical test came on 10 September 2022, when BlueWalker 3 launched from Cape Canaveral. Two months later AST announced that the satellite had deployed its 693-square-foot communications array in orbit. BlueWalker 3 was not built to be a revenue satellite. It was built to answer the question on which the whole company rested: whether a standard phone on the ground could maintain a broadband-quality link with a fast-moving satellite hundreds of kilometers overhead. [BlueWalker 3 launch](https://ast-science.com/ast-spacemobile-confirms-successful-launch-of-bluewalker-3-into-orbit/); [BlueWalker 3 page](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluewalker-3/)

The answer unfolded across 2023. On 25 April 2023 AST announced the first voice call from space to an ordinary smartphone. On 21 June 2023 it announced the first video call. On 19 September 2023 it announced what it described as the first 5G cellular broadband connection from space to an everyday smartphone, including a measured data rate of 14 Mbps. Those milestones mattered less as public-relations firsts than as successive compression of the technical risk. By the end of 2023, the company could point to direct voice, video and 5G connectivity on standard devices using partner spectrum, rather than to an untested design thesis. [first voice call](https://ast-science.com/2023/04/25/ast-spacemobile-makes-history-in-cellular-connectivity-completing-the-first-ever-space-based-voice-call-using-everyday-unmodified-smartphones/); [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/); [5G milestone](https://ast-science.com/ast-spacemobile-achieves-space-based-5g-cellular-broadband-connectivity-from-everyday-smartphones-another-historic-world-first/)

BlueWalker 3 also exposed an externality that had not been central to the capital-markets story when the company listed: optical brightness. The satellite's large reflective surface made it one of the brighter moving objects in the night sky, prompting academic scrutiny and later company work on reflectivity mitigation. That issue did not break the business model, but it established that scaling the constellation would be judged not only on telecom economics but also on orbital-environment stewardship. [Nature study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06672-7); [Our Responsibility](https://ast-science.com/our-responsibility/)

## BlueBird Block 1: Transition to Operations

On 12 September 2024, a Falcon 9 launched the first five BlueBird satellites, AST's initial commercial fleet. The company later said it completed deployment of the communication phased-array antennas and Q/V antennas in October 2024 and moved into initial validation of the satellites in orbit. Those spacecraft were still far from enough to provide continuous coverage, but they converted AST from a single-prototype company into an operating constellation builder. [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/); [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm)

The commercial architecture around Block 1 was more mature than it had been around BlueWalker 3. January 2024 brought strategic investments from AT&T, Google and Vodafone. May 2024 brought the definitive AT&T commercial agreement and the Verizon partnership with $20 million of prepaid service revenue immediately and a second $45 million payment conditioned on regulatory approvals and a definitive agreement. December 2024 brought Vodafone's definitive long-term commercial agreement through 2034. By the time the five BlueBirds were in orbit, AST had a more formal partner stack and a clearer route from engineering milestones to contractual monetization. [January 2024 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224002914/form8-k.htm); [AT&T agreement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024097099/asts-20240630.htm); [Verizon 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224021726/form8-k.htm); [Vodafone agreement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm)

The operational ramp exposed the next execution question plainly: scaling from five early-commercial satellites to a constellation dense enough to offer continuous, commercially competitive coverage required both the Block 2 programme and sustained capital access. Block 2 satellites, designed with substantially larger antenna apertures — approximately two to three times the area of Block 1 units — would deliver higher per-satellite capacity and improved spectral efficiency, with deployment timelines extending into 2025 and 2026.

## Milestone Chronology

| Era | Date | Event |
|---|---|---|
| Founding | May 2017 | AST & Science founded in Midland, Texas |
| Strategic capital | March 3, 2020 | Rakuten and Vodafone announced as lead investors |
| Public listing | April 7, 2021 | SPAC merger with New Providence; ASTS begins trading |
| Prototype launch | September 10, 2022 | BlueWalker 3 launched aboard Falcon 9 |
| First direct-to-cell voice call | April 25, 2023 | Voice call to ordinary smartphone announced |
| First direct-to-cell video call | June 21, 2023 | Video call to ordinary smartphone announced |
| First direct-to-cell 5G connection | September 19, 2023 | 5G connection announced from BlueWalker 3 |
| First commercial satellites | September 12, 2024 | BlueBird 1-5 launched aboard Falcon 9 |
| First Block 2 satellite | December 23, 2025 | BlueBird 6 launched from India |

From Midland to an operating fleet, the corporate history did not progress linearly. It progressed through proof points: first strategic operators willing to finance the concept, then an on-orbit array large enough to prove the link, then commercial satellites, then a capital stack large enough to attempt constellation scale. What remained by May 2026 was the hardest part: translating technical proof and contractual alignment into continuous coverage and recurring revenue. [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: BlueBird satellites, MNO partnership model, single-product framework
chapters.body:
## A Single Product, Deployed Through Others

AST SpaceMobile was built around a conviction that many in the satellite industry treated as fanciful for years: that a satellite could close a link directly to an ordinary smartphone, with no special hardware on the ground, using the same LTE and 5G spectrum bands that terrestrial carriers had already licensed and deployed. The company's entire commercial architecture flowed from that proposition. From the time Abel Avellan incorporated AST SpaceMobile in Midland, Texas in 2017, through the April 2021 SPAC listing that gave it public-market capital, and into the September 2024 launch of its first operational satellites, the company offered exactly one product to the world: wholesale satellite connectivity, sold to mobile network operators, who would then extend it to their existing subscribers on existing handsets.

That product-market clarity was both a strength and a constraint. AST SpaceMobile held no retail relationships, collected no subscriber data directly, operated no billing infrastructure. What it possessed was the satellite constellation itself, the radio-access technology embedded within it, and the commercial agreements with the operators who held the last-mile relationships at scale. Its revenue, when it arrived, would be a share of what those operators generated from selling coverage to customers who happened to be outside terrestrial signal range.

## The Antenna That Made It Possible

The technology credibility problem AST SpaceMobile faced through its early years was fundamental. Closing a link from low-Earth orbit to a device with the transmit power, antenna gain, and form factor of a consumer handset required satellite antennas of unusual size. The physics were not flexible. A satellite operating at roughly 500 kilometers altitude communicating on cellular bands had to compensate for free-space path loss that dwarfs what a ground tower contends with. The engineering solution Avellan's team developed was the large unfoldable phased-array antenna panel — a structure that could be stowed compactly during launch and then deployed in orbit to dimensions far exceeding any conventional telecommunications satellite.

The BlueWalker 3 prototype, launched in September 2022 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 and into a 500-kilometer orbit, demonstrated the concept at scale for the first time. The satellite carried a 693-square-foot phased-array aperture — at the time of its deployment the largest commercial communications antenna ever operated in LEO. Over the following months it established direct voice calls and broadband data sessions with standard unmodified smartphones, completing a series of milestones the company had told investors to expect but that many in the industry had watched skeptically. The tests used existing cellular spectrum bands, required no firmware changes on the handsets involved, and were conducted in partnership with mobile operators whose spectrum licenses the satellite was operating within. [BlueWalker 3](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluewalker-3/); [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/)

BlueWalker 3 was never intended for commercial service. Its role was validation: of the antenna structure, the phased-array electronics, the thermal management systems, the link budget assumptions that underpinned the entire business case. When the data came back from those tests, AST SpaceMobile's engineering program shifted toward productizing the design into a form that could be manufactured and launched at the scale the constellation required.

## BlueBird Block 1: The Operational Satellite

When AST moved from demonstration hardware to production hardware, it retained that basic design logic. The first five BlueBird satellites launched in September 2024 also carried 693-square-foot arrays, and AST's own product page described them as capable of 40 MHz of bandwidth and 120 Mbps peak transmission speeds per coverage cell. Those were not full-coverage satellites. They were first commercial satellites built to validate the operational version of the model and to support intermittent service in early markets. [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/)

The Block 1 fleet mattered because it shifted the debate from whether the physics worked to whether the network could be operated commercially. AST said the five satellites enabled non-continuous coverage across the United States and select markets, and later highlighted first video calls in Europe, the United States and Japan, as well as later VoLTE milestones with AT&T, Verizon and Bell Canada. In other words, Block 1 was not the end-state network; it was the first on-orbit commercial layer through which operators could test customer experience, core-network integration and spectrum coordination. [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/); [Q1 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025069317/asts-ex99_1.htm)

The September 2024 launch represented a transition from development-stage to early operational status. Five satellites were insufficient for continuous global coverage but sufficient to begin commercial service trials with the carriers that had signed multi-year agreements, and to generate the first data on operational performance at scale — satellite health, link quality across different geographies and atmospheric conditions, handoff behavior, and the performance consistency that carriers would need to validate before configuring their networks to route traffic through AST SpaceMobile's orbital layer.

## Block 2: Scaling Capacity

The next-generation BlueBird satellites were designed to move AST from intermittent service toward continuous service. AST described them as roughly three times larger than Block 1, with about 10 times the data capacity. The company said each next-generation satellite would support 10 GHz of processing bandwidth, more than 2,000 active coverage cells and peak speeds of 120 Mbps per coverage cell. By March 2026 the first unit, BlueBird 6, had been launched and unfolded in orbit; by May 2026 AST said fully assembled microns had been completed for up to 33 BlueBird satellites, including those already shipped or launched. [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/); [How it works](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/our-technology/); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

The scaling logic was explicit in the March 2026 10-Q. AST said it expected noncontinuous service in selected targeted markets with 25 total BlueBird satellites, continuous coverage across key markets with roughly 45 to 60 satellites, and continuous service across all targeted geographies with around 90 satellites. The business model therefore rested on a fairly direct sequence: prove the handset link, prove the operator integration, scale the capacity, then convert contractual relationships into daily usage. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

The transition from Block 1 to Block 2 deployment was therefore the principal scaling event in AST SpaceMobile's forward operational strategy as of the frozen snapshot date. Block 1 established that the system worked in commercial operation; Block 2 was designed to make it work at the throughput volumes that would matter to large carriers managing millions of subscriber minutes.

## The MNO Partnership Model

The commercial architecture AST SpaceMobile constructed around its technology was deliberately indirect. The company sought no direct relationships with the subscribers who would ultimately use its service. Instead, it executed commercial agreements with mobile network operators, under which the operator would market satellite coverage as an extension of its existing plans — and would pay AST SpaceMobile a share of the revenue those customers generated while connected through the satellite layer.

The appeal to operators was coverage without the capital expenditure of tower build-out. Terrestrial network densification in rural or remote areas had long been challenged by the economics of per-subscriber returns against cell tower construction and maintenance costs. AST SpaceMobile offered an alternative: operators could extend their coverage footprints to geographies they had never covered, using a wholesale arrangement that aligned AST SpaceMobile's revenue to actual traffic rather than requiring operators to pay fixed capacity fees regardless of demand.

Commercially, AST remained a layer inside someone else's retail brand. The company said it now had nearly 60 mobile network operator relationships covering more than 3 billion subscribers. The definitive AT&T agreement gave AST a percentage of gross monthly revenue billed by AT&T for services enabled by the satellite layer, while Vodafone's definitive agreement established the framework for space-based cellular broadband across Vodafone home markets and partner markets. Verizon entered first with prepaid commercial commitments and convertible financing, then with a definitive agreement in October 2025. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm); [AT&T Commercial Agreement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024097099/asts-20240630.htm); [Vodafone agreement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm); [2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000006/asts-20251231.htm)

By the frozen snapshot, the partner map had broadened beyond the original anchor names. AST's May 2026 release referenced agreements with Telus in Canada and Axian Telecom in Africa in addition to Bell Canada, Vodacom, Orange and MTN. The June 2025 and year-end disclosures also pointed to relationships across more than 50 MNOs with nearly 3 billion subscribers, while the May 2026 release moved that language to nearly 60 operators and more than 3 billion subscribers. The broad point held across those filings: AST was not trying to win one carrier and then expand. It was trying to create a carrier-neutral wholesale layer that could be switched on across a large installed base once coverage became commercially usable. [Q2 2025 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025106627/asts-20250630.htm); [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

| Partner | Geography | Capital relationship |
|---|---|---|
| AT&T | United States | Strategic investor and definitive commercial agreement |
| Verizon | United States | Prepaid commercial commitments and convertible-note investment; definitive agreement signed in 2025 |
| Vodafone | Europe and Africa | Strategic investor; definitive long-term agreement; SatCo JV |
| Rakuten Mobile | Japan | Strategic investor and commercial partner |
| Bell Canada / Telus | Canada | Commercial partners |
| MTN / Vodacom / Orange / Axian | Africa and other markets | Commercial partners |

The equity stakes held by Vodafone and Rakuten were not incidental. They reflected the depth of strategic alignment those partners had made with AST SpaceMobile's trajectory — a financial bet on the technology alongside the commercial one, which carried different implications for the durability of the commercial relationships than a standard wholesale agreement might.

## What the Framework Excludes

The important correction, as of May 2026, was that AST was no longer a pure future-retail story. It still had no direct consumer billing relationship and no handset business, but it had begun recognizing revenue from gateway deliveries, government milestones and other operator-linked arrangements before continuous consumer coverage existed. The filings were also clear that the company designed the network for both commercial and government applications. What remained excluded was a direct-to-consumer model: AST was still building a wholesale satellite extension to terrestrial carriers, not a consumer telecom brand of its own. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

That bet would be tested as BlueBird Block 2 deployment proceeded and the first full revenue cycles from AT&T and Verizon agreements moved from service trials toward commercial volume.

chapters.title: Pre-commercial revenue, capital raises, and the constellation deployment economics
chapters.body:
## Engineering services and the revenue paradox of early deployment

AST SpaceMobile's reported revenue history looked very different from the one often implied in broad-brush summaries of the company. In 2022 the company reported $13.8 million of revenue, but the 2022 10-K made clear that this came from its former subsidiary NanoAvionika UAB, which generated revenue from the development and manufacture of satellite technology and related services before AST sold its 51% interest in September 2022. After that sale, the company said in its 2023 filings that it no longer generated revenue and did not expect to generate revenue until the launch of SpaceMobile Service. The result was stark: 2023 revenue was zero. [2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017023011124/asts-20221231.htm); [2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024039342/asts-20231231.htm)

That distinction mattered because it changed the meaning of the company's early top line. Revenue in 2022 was not evidence that the direct-to-cell constellation had begun to monetize. It was the tail of a now-divested satellite-manufacturing subsidiary. The cleanest way to read AST's operating history was therefore as a company that had meaningful legacy revenue in 2022, no operating revenue from its core direct-to-cell thesis in 2023, a modest but real return of revenue in 2024 from government and gateway work, and a larger 2025 step-up as operator and government contracts began to show up in reported numbers. [2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017023011124/asts-20221231.htm); [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm)

## 2024 and 2025: The Return of Revenue

The 2024 10-K said AST recognized $4.4 million of revenue during the year ended 31 December 2024: $3.9 million from performance obligations completed under agreements with prime contractors for U.S. government contracts and $0.5 million from resale of gateway equipment to a mobile network operator. That was not mass-market cellular revenue, but it was no longer zero. It showed that the company had begun to monetize parts of the network build-out before continuous service existed. [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm)

The bigger jump came in 2025. AST reported $70.9 million of revenue for the full year, including $44.4 million of product revenue and $26.5 million of services revenue. Management described that 2025 revenue as having been driven by mobile network operator partners and the U.S. government. The first quarter of 2026 then added another $14.7 million, made up of $13.4 million of product revenue and $1.3 million of services revenue, with the company again attributing the figure chiefly to gateway deliveries and government milestones. [2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000006/asts-20251231.htm); [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

| Period | Revenue | What it represented |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | $13.8 million | Legacy NanoAvionika revenue before AST's September 2022 sale of its 51% stake |
| 2023 | $0 | No meaningful revenue after Nano sale and before SpaceMobile launch |
| 2024 | $4.4 million | Government milestone work and gateway equipment resale |
| 2025 | $70.9 million | MNO-partner and U.S. government revenue |
| Q1 2026 | $14.7 million | Gateway deliveries and U.S. government milestones |

## The SPAC and the initial capital stack

AST SpaceMobile reached the public markets on 7 April 2021 through a merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp, a blank-check vehicle that had been assembled specifically to take the Midland, Texas company public. The transaction was structured as a conventional SPAC business combination with a concurrent PIPE placement, and it delivered the proceeds AST needed to move BlueWalker 3 from design to fabrication. The listing placed the company on NASDAQ under the ticker ASTS, and gave it a public currency — critical for subsequent capital formation in an industry where the capital requirements are front-loaded and the revenue curves are long.

The SPAC structure also locked in the first tier of strategic equity. Vodafone and Rakuten Mobile, both of which had signed commercial framework agreements with AST before the listing, retained meaningful stakes through the transaction. Their presence on the cap table served a dual signalling function: it anchored the commercial thesis for public market investors, and it gave AST a cost-of-capital advantage in subsequent raises by demonstrating that sophisticated telecommunications operators were willing to put equity at risk behind the technology.

## Strategic Capital: From Partner Validation to Large-Scale Funding

The capital side of the story was equally milestone-driven. In January 2024 AST announced strategic investments and commercial commitments from AT&T, Google and Vodafone and said that, together with related capital actions, the package could deliver up to $306.5 million of aggregate gross proceeds. The underlying investment agreement covered $110 million of subordinated convertible notes purchased by AT&T, Google and Vodafone. This was not ordinary financing: it was capital attached to commercial and technical alignment. [January 2024 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224002914/form8-k.htm); [Q1 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024060499/asts-20240331.htm)

In May 2024 Verizon added another strategic layer. The company's 2024 disclosures said Verizon's partnership represented a $100 million financial commitment, composed of $65 million of commercial prepayments and $35 million of convertible notes. The formal memorandum of understanding also provided for an initial $20 million commercial payment, which AST said it had received and recorded as a contract liability, and a second $45 million commercial payment contingent on regulatory approvals and a definitive commercial agreement. [Verizon 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224021726/form8-k.htm); [Q2 2024 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024097095/asts-ex99_1.htm)

Once BlueBird deployment became real, the financing scale increased. AST issued $460 million of 4.25% convertible senior notes in January 2025, $575 million of 2.375% convertible senior notes in July 2025, $1.15 billion of 2.00% convertible senior notes in October 2025, and $1.075 billion of 2.25% convertible senior notes in February 2026 including the exercised additional-notes option. The company also repurchased portions of earlier convertible issues in 2025 and early 2026, turning what had begun as a relatively simple capital story into a layered liability structure with multiple coupons, conversion prices and maturity dates. [January 2025 notes](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315225003793/ex99-1.htm); [July 2025 notes 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225021421/form8-k.htm); [2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000006/asts-20251231.htm); [February 2026 notes 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315226007626/form8-k.htm)

Rakuten Mobile's position reflected a different strategic rationale. The Japanese carrier, which operates a cloud-native terrestrial network under Tarō Kono's reform-era mobile liberalisation, had identified AST's coverage extension capability as a way to address Japan's substantial unserved rural geography without the capital intensity of additional ground infrastructure. Its equity position thus functioned simultaneously as a hedge against coverage cost and a strategic option on the satellite layer of a future converged network.

## Subsequent capital raises: feeding the constellation machine

The SPAC proceeds were never intended to fund full-constellation deployment. The architecture of AST's financing strategy depended on milestone-gated capital formation: demonstrate the technology, sign the MNO agreements, build investor conviction, then raise larger tranches at progressively more advantageous terms as the risk profile compressed. That logic held, if imperfectly.

The company executed multiple equity offerings between 2021 and 2024, taking advantage of periods of elevated share price — particularly following positive BlueWalker 3 test results in late 2022 and early 2023, when the satellite established direct voice calls to unmodified smartphones and set records for data throughput in the direct-to-cell segment. Each successful demonstration gave AST a window to raise at terms that diluted existing holders less than the capital would otherwise have cost.

The combined effect of these instruments was a capital structure that, by mid-2024, was substantially more complex than the clean equity-only balance sheet the SPAC had produced three years earlier. Warrants, convertible instruments, and multiple tranches of common stock issued at varying prices created a layered equity overhang that market participants tracked carefully as a potential headwind against share price appreciation in the commercial phase.

## Operating economics and the cost of pre-commercial scale

AST's operating losses over the 2022–2024 period were substantial and structurally predictable. The company was simultaneously carrying the capital expenditure of satellite manufacturing — a programme with no comparable cost-reduction roadmap to SpaceX's Falcon 9 amortisation, though it benefited from using SpaceX as its launch provider — and the operating expenditure of a growing engineering organisation in Midland, Texas, where it had expanded its antenna fabrication and testing capabilities, and in Midland and internationally where it maintained its software and network engineering teams.

Research and development expenditure dominated the income statement below the revenue line. The development of BlueWalker 3, its integration and testing campaign, the redesign work that produced the BlueBird platform architecture, and the further scaling effort behind the next-generation BlueBird design all required sustained engineering headcount and equipment spending well ahead of any consumer-service revenue. By the frozen window AST was no longer describing Block 2 in vague relative terms. It was describing a fleet with nearly 2,400 square feet of phased array, roughly three times the size of Block 1 and about 10 times the data capacity. [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/); [How it works](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/our-technology/)

Stock-based compensation, a standard feature of the pre-revenue technology company income statement, added a non-cash layer to reported losses that inflated the headline figure without affecting the cash burn that mattered most to the runway calculation. On a cash basis, AST was burning at a rate that made its capital raise cadence structurally necessary rather than opportunistic.

## Liquidity, Backlog, and Constellation Funding

The economics of deploying a low earth orbit satellite constellation at commercial scale are not linear. The per-satellite manufacturing cost carries significant fixed overhead in the early production batches, where tooling, test infrastructure, and engineering iteration dominate unit economics. As production volumes increase, the learning curve and supply chain maturation compress per-unit costs — a dynamic that AST was actively pursuing as it moved toward Block 2.

Launch costs were no longer only a SpaceX question. AST had signed a multi-launch agreement with SpaceX in March 2022, used Falcon 9 for BlueWalker 3 and BlueBird 1-5, launched BlueBird 6 on ISRO's LVM3 in December 2025, and then lost BlueBird 7 after Blue Origin's New Glenn upper-stage anomaly in April 2026. That diversification did not eliminate launch-cost risk, but it did mean the company's deployment plan was no longer tied to a single launch provider or a single manifest assumption. [SpaceX multi-launch agreement](https://ast-science.com/2022/03/09/ast-spacemobile-announces-multi-launch-agreement-with-spacex/); [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/); [BlueBird 7 update](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315226018012/ex99-1.htm)

Block 2's larger physical footprint implied higher per-satellite manufacturing cost relative to Block 1, but AST's own disclosures framed the trade as one of capacity and service continuity rather than simple hardware inflation. The March 2026 10-Q said the company expected 25 total satellites to support noncontinuous service in selected targeted markets, roughly 45 to 60 satellites for continuous coverage across key markets, and about 90 satellites for continuous service across all targeted geographies. The economic logic of the larger satellite therefore rested on reducing the number of satellites required per commercially useful coverage layer even as each unit cost more to build. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

AST's headline liquidity position was large by pre-commercial space-company standards. The March 2026 10-Q said cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash totaled $3.4589 billion, including roughly $429.3 million of restricted cash. The same filing said remaining performance obligations were approximately $1.2 billion as of 31 March 2026. Management also told investors it believed the company was fully funded for the costs necessary to manufacture and launch a constellation of approximately 90 BlueBird satellites. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

But "fully funded" did not mean fully finished. The same filing said AST still expected to need 25 satellites for noncontinuous service in targeted markets, 45 to 60 for continuous coverage across key markets, and about 90 for continuous service across all targeted geographies. It also warned that average capital cost could rise materially if the company failed to achieve supply-chain diversification, cost reductions, process improvements or favorable launch contracts. The financing architecture was therefore better read as a bridge to the first large commercial constellation, not as the end of the capital question. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

| Capital Event | Timing | Strategic significance |
|---|---|---|
| SPAC merger + PIPE | April 2021 | Initial public-market capital and listed equity currency |
| Strategic investments + related capital actions | January 2024 | AT&T, Google and Vodafone package described as worth up to $306.5 million in gross proceeds |
| Verizon partnership commitment | May 2024 | $65 million of prepaid commercial commitments plus $35 million of convertible notes |
| 4.25% convertible senior notes | January 2025 | $460 million raised for constellation build-out |
| 2.375% convertible senior notes | July 2025 | $575 million raised |
| 2.00% convertible senior notes | October 2025 | $1.15 billion raised |
| 2.25% convertible senior notes | February 2026 | $1.075 billion raised, including the exercised option for additional notes |

The financial core of the AST story, then, was no longer a simple "pre-revenue" narrative. It was a transitional one: legacy Nano revenue in 2022, a zero-revenue reset in 2023, government and gateway revenue in 2024, a more meaningful partner-and-government ramp in 2025, and a March 2026 balance sheet large enough to finance an aggressive next stage but still dependent on execution. [2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017023011124/asts-20221231.htm); [2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024039342/asts-20231231.htm); [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: Post-SPAC quarters through BlueWalker, BlueBird, and MNO partnership milestones
chapters.body:
## The SPAC Debut and the Weight of the Promise

When AST SpaceMobile completed its business combination with New Providence Acquisition Corp in April 2021, investors were buying into a milestone sequence rather than a mature telecom income statement. The immediate post-listing period therefore offered little help from conventional earnings analysis. What mattered first was whether BlueWalker 3 would fly and deploy; only after that would operator agreements, gateway economics and recurring usage become meaningful. The revenue history that later emerged was also more uneven than early shorthand suggested: 2022 revenue was $13.8 million from the legacy NanoAvionika subsidiary, 2023 revenue fell to zero after AST sold its 51% Nano stake, 2024 revenue returned at $4.4 million from U.S. government milestones and gateway resale, and 2025 revenue rose to $70.9 million before the first quarter of 2026 added $14.7 million. [ASTS listing announcement](https://ast-science.com/2021/04/06/nasdaq-asts/); [2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017023011124/asts-20221231.htm); [2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024039342/asts-20231231.htm); [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm); [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

The investor communications from the first post-SPAC quarters carried the structural tension inherent to any pre-commercial infrastructure company in a growth phase. Avellan and CFO Andrew Johnson articulated the strategic case in terms of total addressable market — roughly five billion people with limited or no mobile broadband connectivity — against a timeline requiring both technical execution of a novel satellite design and commercial alignment with global mobile network operators. The financial profile provided little to evaluate beyond the scale of operating losses; the investment case rested on the technology's credibility, which only a flight demonstration could establish.

## BlueWalker 3: Proof of Physics

The single most consequential event in the post-SPAC period was the launch of the BlueWalker 3 test satellite aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 on September 10, 2022. BlueWalker 3 was not a commercial satellite but a full-scale prototype — a platform designed to validate the core technical claims underpinning the entire business model. The satellite carried an approximately 693-square-foot (64 square metre) phased-array antenna that, upon deployment in late October 2022, constituted the largest commercial communications array placed in low Earth orbit to that date. The engineering challenge was exacting: to serve standard unmodified handsets, the satellite needed to replicate, from roughly 500 kilometres altitude, the signal characteristics that a terrestrial cell tower provides metres from the user.

Around the September 2022 launch, AST positioned BlueWalker 3 as the foundation of its plan to provide broadband to unserved and underserved communities through standard smartphones, with no new hardware required. That framing mattered because the earnings story was still almost entirely a technology-credibility story. Until the satellite unfolded and worked, the income statement could not do the persuasion on its own. [BlueWalker 3 launch](https://ast-science.com/ast-spacemobile-confirms-successful-launch-of-bluewalker-3-into-orbit/)

That first pivotal milestone came in September 2022 with the BlueWalker 3 launch and in November 2022 with the deployment of its 693-square-foot array. The next set of investor inflection points followed quickly: voice call in April 2023, video call in June 2023, and 5G connectivity in September 2023. The shift in the earnings story was subtle but real. AST's quarterly discussion no longer centered only on what management believed might work; it centered on a prototype that had already proven core claims in orbit. [BlueWalker 3](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluewalker-3/); [first voice call](https://ast-science.com/2023/04/25/ast-spacemobile-makes-history-in-cellular-connectivity-completing-the-first-ever-space-based-voice-call-using-everyday-unmodified-smartphones/); [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/)

Those milestones gave management something more concrete than addressable-market rhetoric. By the end of 2023 the investor narrative had shifted from whether the link budget might work to what constellation scale, spectrum access and capital would be required to turn the demonstrated handset link into a revenue network. [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/)

## The Partnership Architecture Solidifies

The period between the BlueWalker 3 demonstrations and the BlueBird Block 1 launch was defined less by revenue than by the expansion of the mobile network operator partnership framework. The strategic logic was structural: AST SpaceMobile did not intend to serve end users directly. The SpaceMobile network would operate as a supplemental layer on top of existing MNO networks, with MNO partners providing spectrum and customer relationships while AST provided the space segment.

By 2025 and early 2026 the company was describing a partner ecosystem of nearly 60 mobile network operators covering more than 3 billion subscribers, rather than a smaller pre-Block 1 roster that could be summarized as a handful of flagship logos. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

| MNO / strategic partner | Geography | Capital or contract note |
|---|---|---|
| AT&T | United States | Strategic investor and definitive commercial agreement through 2030 |
| Verizon | United States | $65 million of prepayments and $35 million of notes in 2024; definitive agreement signed in 2025 |
| Vodafone | Europe and Africa | Strategic investor; definitive long-term commercial agreement; SatCo structure |
| Rakuten Mobile | Japan | Strategic investor and commercial partner |
| Bell Canada / Telus | Canada | Commercial partners |
| Orange / Telefonica / MTN and others | International | Broader commercial partner base across nearly 60 MNO relationships |

The equity and financing structure around those partnerships also became more precise over time. Vodafone and Rakuten were the earlier strategic holders. AT&T and Google joined the January 2024 investment package. Verizon's role was better described as strategic financing and prepayments than as conventional board-represented equity. What tied the group together was less a uniform security than a shared commercial interest in making satellite service work on licensed cellular spectrum. [January 2024 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224002914/form8-k.htm); [Verizon 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224021726/form8-k.htm); [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225006182/formdef14a.htm)

The company's balance-sheet management through this period reflected the challenge of funding a capital-intensive constellation on only early, uneven revenue. The critical correction is that the 2022 and 2023 figures were not recurring consumer-service revenue, and the 2024 number was not a simple continuation of engineering-services revenue. The business was moving from legacy Nano revenue to a zero-revenue reset, then to government and gateway revenue, and only later toward partner-linked commercial receipts. [2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017023011124/asts-20221231.htm); [2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024039342/asts-20231231.htm); [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm)

## BlueBird Block 1: Transition to Operations

The September 2024 BlueBird launch changed the quarterly narrative again. The company now had commercial satellites in orbit, even if it did not yet have continuous coverage. Its 2024 revenue remained modest because continuous mass-market service had not started, but the launch itself created the bridge to the next set of operating milestones: first video calls in Europe, the United States and Japan on Block 1 satellites; first VoLTE calls with AT&T and Verizon core networks; and a growing set of government use cases. [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/); [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/)

AST described that September 2024 launch as the transition from technology demonstration toward commercial operations, but the earnings consequence was still staged rather than immediate. The satellites created the bridge to later operating milestones; they did not yet create continuous consumer coverage. [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/); [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/)

The reported numbers across that period also needed careful reading. Revenue in 2022 was $13.8 million, but it was legacy Nano revenue. After AST sold its 51% stake in Nano in September 2022, 2023 revenue fell to zero. Revenue returned in 2024 at $4.4 million, overwhelmingly from U.S. government milestones and gateway resale, then climbed to $70.9 million in 2025. By the first quarter of 2026 AST was reporting $14.7 million of quarterly revenue and telling investors that the business was following its planned revenue ramp during 2026 even before full continuous commercial service existed. [2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017023011124/asts-20221231.htm); [2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024039342/asts-20231231.htm); [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm); [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

## Toward Commercial Scale: Q4 2024 Through Q1 2026

By the time AST reported fourth-quarter and full-year 2025 results on 2 March 2026, the company was no longer presenting itself merely as a prototype success. It reported $70.9 million of full-year revenue, more than $1.2 billion of aggregate contracted revenue commitments, and a launch roadmap intended to reach 45 to 60 satellites in orbit by the end of 2026. Two months later, the first-quarter 2026 release added an FCC SCS authorization for U.S. commercial service, nearly 60 operator partners covering more than 3 billion subscribers, and a mid-June launch plan for BlueBird 8, 9 and 10, while the 10-Q translated the broader constellation plan into threshold numbers of 25, 45 to 60 and about 90 satellites. [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

Avellan's investor communications through Q4 2024 and across 2025 returned repeatedly to the structural commercial proposition: direct-to-cell operated in the cellular bands licensed to MNO partners rather than requiring dedicated spectrum allocations or specialist handset hardware, offering a unit economics argument that conventional satellite broadband models could not replicate for the mass-market mobile use case.

Through the frozen snapshot, the quarterly story had therefore become less speculative but not yet stable. The company had crossed the line from proof satellite to commercial satellite, from zero revenue to meaningful but still early revenue, and from broad MOU language to a more developed operator-contract stack. What it had not yet crossed was the line from intermittent coverage and milestone revenue into a fully continuous consumer service at scale. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: Abel Avellan, executives, and the MNO-investor board
chapters.body:
## Founder-Led Control With a More Conventional Operating Bench

As of the frozen snapshot, AST SpaceMobile remained unmistakably founder-led. The company's governance pages and 2025 proxy identified Abel Avellan as founder, chairman and chief executive officer; Scott Wisniewski as president and chief strategy officer; Andrew Johnson as chief financial officer and chief legal officer; Shanti Gupta as chief operating officer; and Dr. Huiwen Yao as chief technology officer. The broader disclosed senior bench also included John Slamecka as executive adviser to the chairman, Chris Ivory as chief commercial officer, J.R. Wilson as chief of networks and spectrum, Jennifer Manner on regulatory affairs, and production and operations leaders across the Midland build-out. [Leadership and governance](https://investors.ast-science.com/committee-composition); [Management team](https://ast-science.com/investors/governance/management-team/)

The company's 2025 proxy also made a more pointed compensation disclosure: Avellan received no base salary in 2022, 2023 or 2024. For a capital-intensive, pre-commercial company still dependent on repeated fund-raising, that zero-salary position read as a deliberate governance signal of alignment, even if the far larger economic exposure remained his equity and voting control. [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225006182/formdef14a.htm)

## Board Structure and Strategic Representation

The 2025 proxy said the board consisted of 12 directors with one seat vacant, and listed the seated directors as Abel Avellan, Adriana Cisneros, Luke Ibbetson, Andrew Johnson, Edward Knapp, Keith Larson, Hiroshi Mikitani, Ronald Rubin, Richard Sarnoff, Julio A. Torres and Johan Wibergh. The same proxy said five of those directors qualified as independent. The composition was not accidental. It reflected the negotiated cap table around AST: Vodafone, American Tower, AT&T, Rakuten, Antares and Avellan all had rights under the stockholders' agreement, subject to ownership and other conditions. [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225006182/formdef14a.htm)

That structure meant the board blended telecom and infrastructure partners with traditional independents. Luke Ibbetson came from Vodafone, Edward Knapp from American Tower, Hiroshi Mikitani from Rakuten, and Keith Larson filled the AT&T designee seat. Julio Torres served as lead independent director, while Richard Sarnoff and Ronald Rubin brought private-equity and telecom-infrastructure experience. Cisneros represented the long-standing Antares relationship, and Andrew Johnson held the unusual dual position of senior operating executive and director. [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225006182/formdef14a.htm); [Leadership and governance](https://investors.ast-science.com/committee-composition)

## The AT&T Seat Change in 2025

One board change during the frozen window was especially precise in the filings. On 29 January 2025, Christopher Sambar notified AST that he was resigning from the board as AT&T's designee. The same 8-K said the decision did not arise from any disagreement with the company. On the same date, and effective 30 January 2025, the board appointed Keith Larson, upon AT&T's nomination, to fill the vacancy created by Sambar's resignation. That filing gave the turnover a matter-of-fact tone: it read more as a seat transfer inside the AT&T relationship than as a dispute or strategic fracture. [January 2025 board-change 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315225004602/form8-k.htm)

## Executive Turnover in 2024

The proxy also clarified two other personnel changes that earlier summaries often blurred. Sean Wallace, the former chief financial officer, retired from that position in June 2024. Brian Heller, the former general counsel and secretary, left the company in May 2024. Both men still appeared in the proxy as former named executive officers for 2024 compensation disclosure purposes, which mattered because it showed the company treating those departures as part of its disclosed executive transition rather than as off-cycle personnel noise. [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225006182/formdef14a.htm)

What emerged by May 2026 was therefore a governance structure that remained centralized at the top but had become more operationally conventional below it. Avellan still dominated the strategic identity of AST. But the day-to-day operating bench and the board's committee structure looked more like that of a telecom-infrastructure company with heavyweight strategic backers than that of a one-man founder venture. [Leadership and governance](https://investors.ast-science.com/committee-composition); [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225006182/formdef14a.htm)

chapters.title: AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, broader MNO portfolio, and the satellite supply chain
chapters.body:
## The operator alliance: building the wholesale satellite layer

AST's commercial asset sat less in a consumer brand than in its operator stack. By the frozen snapshot the company said its commercial ecosystem had expanded to nearly 60 mobile network operators covering more than 3 billion subscribers. That mattered because AST was not trying to replace national carriers. It was trying to make itself useful to them in the places where terrestrial economics failed. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

The architecture is wholesale, not retail. AST does not sell directly to consumers, does not build handsets, and does not operate billing infrastructure. Instead, it sells satellite connectivity as a layer that mobile operators embed into their existing networks — subscribers connect to BlueBird satellites using the same smartphones and the same SIM cards they already carry, billed through their existing carrier accounts. The MNO assumes the customer relationship; AST provides the coverage infrastructure. This model required that AST secure MNO partners before it could demonstrate commercial service, making the partnership portfolio the commercial asset in the same way that tower companies treat their tenancy agreements.

## AT&T and Verizon: spectrum anchor and US commercial cornerstone

The AT&T relationship was the most clearly documented U.S. commercial contract. AST disclosed that AST LLC and AT&T Services entered into their space-based wireless connectivity agreement on 10 May 2024. Under that agreement, AT&T would purchase access to AST's network and pay AST a percentage of the gross monthly revenue billed to end users for the satellite-enabled service, plus a non-refundable commercial payment after the successful launch and initial operation of the five Block 1 satellites. The agreement ran through 31 December 2030, subject to auto-renewal. AST and AT&T also used the relationship to push public-safety and FirstNet testing before mass commercial service existed. [AT&T Commercial Agreement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024097099/asts-20240630.htm); [AT&T / FirstNet](https://ast-science.com/2024/04/04/att-and-ast-spacemobile-explore-pioneering-satellite-connectivity-for-firstnet/)

Verizon's path was slightly different. AST's May 2024 disclosure said Verizon's partnership represented a $100 million commitment composed of $65 million of commercial prepayments and $35 million of convertible notes. The memorandum of understanding provided for an initial $20 million prepaid commercial payment, which AST said it had received, and a second $45 million payment contingent on regulatory approvals and a definitive commercial agreement. By October 2025 the definitive agreement had been signed, and AST's 2025 filings said the service was intended to begin in 2026 for Verizon customers in the continental United States excluding Alaska and Hawaii. [Verizon 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224021726/form8-k.htm); [2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000006/asts-20251231.htm)

AST SpaceMobile's satellites did not use dedicated satellite spectrum allocations. Instead, they operated in the same LTE frequency bands — including AWS, PCS, and 700 MHz bands — that AT&T and Verizon held through their terrestrial licenses. The technical and regulatory insight behind the company's founding was that a satellite carrying a sufficiently large phased-array antenna could concentrate radio energy precisely enough to illuminate a standard handset using these existing bands without causing unacceptable interference to the terrestrial networks beneath. The spectrum coordination between satellite and ground was managed jointly between AST and the carrier partners.

The practical significance of those carrier relationships extended beyond direct contract economics. AT&T's investment and board-designee rights aligned a major U.S. carrier directly with AST's regulatory progress, while Verizon's prepayments and convertible financing created a different but still material incentive for the second-largest U.S. wireless carrier to support commercial rollout. The alignment was real, but it was not accurate to describe both carriers simply as pre-SPAC equity backers. [January 2024 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224002914/form8-k.htm); [Verizon 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224021726/form8-k.htm); [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000164117225006182/formdef14a.htm)

## Vodafone and Rakuten: strategic anchors in international markets

Vodafone's role ran deeper than a simple distribution agreement. It was an investor, a board-level presence and, by December 2024, AST's counterparty in a definitive long-term commercial agreement through 2034. That agreement established a framework for Vodafone to offer space-based cellular broadband in its home markets and through its Partner Markets program, with mutual exclusivity in certain circumstances, preferential commercial terms, revenue share, and ground-station responsibilities. In March 2025 the relationship moved another step with the announced SatCo joint venture, later described in AST's filings as the exclusive European distribution vehicle for SpaceMobile Service in Europe, the UK and certain other markets. [Vodafone agreement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm); [SatCo disclosure](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315225011388/form424b5.htm); [2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000006/asts-20251231.htm)

Rakuten was the older strategic anchor. It had been one of the lead investors announced in March 2020, and AST continued to use the relationship as both capital validation and market access in Japan. In April 2025, AST said it had completed Japan's first space-based video call using a standard smartphone together with Rakuten Mobile. [Rakuten and Vodafone investment](https://ast-science.com/2020/03/03/rakuten-vodafone-invest-in-ast/); [Q1 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025069317/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/)

Rakuten Mobile's partnership occupied a different strategic position. The Japanese carrier, which launched Japan's first cloud-native, fully virtualised mobile network in 2020, brought engineering credibility and a specific market advantage: Japan's regulatory environment for satellite services had historically been cautious, and Rakuten's domestic sponsorship smoothed the approval pathway. Rakuten's investment in AST reflected a broader thesis about low-Earth-orbit connectivity filling the rural and suburban coverage gaps that Rakuten's still-maturing 4G network had not fully closed. Like Vodafone, Rakuten held equity and contributed access to Japan's frequency bands — making its partnership simultaneously financial and operational.

## The broader MNO portfolio: 50 countries and counting

The partner list broadened beyond the flagship names.
