AST's recent disclosures referenced Bell Canada, Telus, Orange, MTN, Vodacom and Axian Telecom, while its public partner materials also highlighted Bell and other carrier relationships as central to the network's geographic reach. The 2025 year-end release added Orange, Telefonica, CK Hutchison, Taiwan Mobile and Sunrise to the list of expanded commercial partnerships. The pattern was clear: AST was trying to assemble regional density rather than a handful of symbolic logos. [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Partners](https://ast-science.com/company/mobile-network-operators/)

MTN Group, the Johannesburg-headquartered pan-African carrier with operations across more than twenty African markets, represented arguably the single largest addressable population among AST's MNO partners. Sub-Saharan Africa's mobile penetration rate — already among the fastest growing in the world — masked a structural coverage problem: the continent's population density patterns made terrestrial infrastructure economics unworkable across large rural and peri-urban areas. MTN's partnership with AST was an acknowledgment that satellite-layer wholesale coverage could close gaps that MTN's own capital expenditure programme could not economically address.

The cumulative geographic reach of the MNO portfolio therefore became more concrete by the frozen window than older drafts suggested. AST's May 2026 release said the company had nearly 60 operator relationships covering more than 3 billion subscribers. That figure mattered because it showed that the commercial question was no longer whether AST could sign carriers at all; it was whether AST could launch enough satellites to make the existing carrier stack commercially useful often enough to matter. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

## Satellite manufacturing: phased-array engineering at scale in Midland

The physical expression of AST SpaceMobile's technological ambition was the BlueBird satellite, built principally at the company's Midland, Texas facility. The defining engineering challenge was the phased-array antenna: to illuminate a standard smartphone from low Earth orbit, the satellite must concentrate radio energy with extraordinary precision, which in practice required an antenna aperture measured in tens of square metres.

The supply-chain story also looked more mature by March 2026 than some earlier summaries suggested. AST told investors that it had completed planned investments to reach capacity to assemble, integrate and test up to six Block 2 satellites per month. It said supplier agreements and orders were in place for materials and components needed for a large majority of the planned constellation of more than 90 BlueBird satellites, and that fully assembled microns had been completed for up to 33 BlueBird satellites including those already shipped or launched. AST's public site separately described nearly 500,000 square feet of production facilities and roughly 95% vertical integration on BlueBird 1-5. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm); [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/); [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/)

Manufacturing the phased-array antenna required integrating thousands of individual radiating elements into a structure capable of surviving launch loads, deploying reliably in the thermal extremes of low Earth orbit, and maintaining phase coherence across the full aperture throughout operations. AST developed the phased-array design internally, treating it as a core proprietary asset, while sourcing other bus components — solar arrays, reaction wheels, propulsion systems, star trackers — from specialist suppliers. The Midland facility combined satellite assembly with antenna fabrication, a degree of vertical integration reflecting both the novelty of the antenna technology and the absence of any off-the-shelf supplier capable of delivering phased arrays at the required scale.

## Launch services: SpaceX as infrastructure partner

SpaceX was important, but it was no longer the whole launch story. AST had entered a multi-launch agreement with SpaceX in March 2022, used Falcon 9 for BlueWalker 3 and BlueBird 1-5, and continued to rely on Falcon 9 for subsequent campaigns. But BlueBird 6 went up on ISRO's LVM3 in December 2025, and BlueBird 7 launched on Blue Origin's New Glenn in April 2026 before being lost because of the upper-stage anomaly. That diversification mattered strategically: AST remained exposed to Falcon 9 scheduling, but by the frozen snapshot it had already demonstrated willingness to use multiple launch providers. [SpaceX multi-launch agreement](https://ast-science.com/2022/03/09/ast-spacemobile-announces-multi-launch-agreement-with-spacex/); [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/); [BlueBird 7 update](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315226018012/ex99-1.htm)

The relationship with SpaceX carried competitive complexity that investors did not overlook. SpaceX's own Starlink Direct to Cell programme — a direct-to-device service built on the Starlink constellation in commercial partnership with T-Mobile — competed in the same market segment as AST and used the same Falcon 9 for its own launches. AST was simultaneously dependent on a competitor's launch infrastructure and contesting that competitor's satellite service offering. Avellan addressed the distinction in investor forums by emphasising that AST's MNO-neutral wholesale model — serving AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, and dozens of other carriers rather than a single operator — created a broader commercial addressable market than any service tied to one carrier's subscriber base.

## Regulatory architecture: FCC, ITU, and the spectrum coordination framework

The regulatory stack had grown more concrete by May 2026. AST's first-quarter release said the FCC had authorized commercial SpaceMobile Service in the United States with a grant of Supplemental Coverage from Space authority. The 10-Q said the company had received FCC authorization to deploy a 248-satellite network, including domestic and international low-band IMT terrestrial frequencies and Q/V-band feeder links, and also said AST expected long-term access to up to 45 MHz of lower mid-band spectrum in the United States and Canada through the Ligado term sheet signed in January 2025. Those were still not a substitute for approvals in every non-U.S. jurisdiction, but they materially improved the legal scaffolding around the commercial story. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

Internationally, the International Telecommunication Union's coordination procedures governed AST's ability to operate in partner-country frequency bands without causing harmful interference to other licensed systems. Each MNO partnership carried implicit spectrum rights — the carrier's domestic licenses extended, through the AST commercial agreement and applicable national regulation, to cover satellite-layer transmissions in that carrier's frequency bands. The ITU filing position for AST's satellite network, maintained through the coordination process, underpinned the legal certainty that investors and commercial partners required before committing capital to a deployment programme eventually measured in hundreds of satellites.

chapters.title: Where AST sits against Starlink Direct to Cell, Lynk Global, and broader satellite competitors
chapters.body:
## A Market That Looked Uncontested, Then Didn't

When Abel Avellan assembled the first engineering team in Midland, Texas in 2017, direct-to-cell satellite connectivity for unmodified smartphones was a concept that the industry's incumbents had largely dismissed as physically impossible. The link budget arithmetic seemed unforgiving: a handheld device radiating a fraction of a watt against the vacuum of low-Earth orbit, with no dish, no special firmware, no cooperative ground infrastructure. By the time BlueWalker 3 demonstrated two-way voice and data in late 2022, the premise had shifted from improbable to proven — and the competitive map shifted with it.

The company that had spent five years building toward a largely uncontested market found itself, by 2024, in a three-front competitive environment: SpaceX's Starlink Direct to Cell program scaling aggressively; Lynk Global pursuing a narrowband niche from a well-funded private position; and Apple's emergency satellite feature quietly redefining consumer expectations without ever targeting broadband. Each competitor illuminated a different dimension of what AST was actually selling, and what it was not.

## Starlink Direct to Cell: The Scaled Threat

The most consequential competitive move came from SpaceX and T-Mobile. SpaceX said in January 2024 that it had sent and received first text messages using T-Mobile spectrum through newly launched direct-to-cell satellites. T-Mobile later said T-Satellite would launch nationwide on 23 July 2025 and that more than 657 Starlink direct-to-cell satellites were already in orbit at launch. The launch feature set was narrower than full broadband - SMS on iOS and Android, MMS and picture messaging, and short audio clips for Android, with later expansion into data-capable apps - but the commercial significance was obvious: a competing space-to-phone service reached paying customers before AST had continuous consumer coverage. [Starlink first-text update](https://starlink.com/public-files/DIRECT_TO_CELL_FIRST_TEXT_UPDATE.pdf); [T-Mobile launch](https://www.t-mobile.com/news/network/best-network-in-america); [T-Satellite available](https://www.t-mobile.com/news/network/t-satellite-now-available)

By April 2026 the regulatory tailwind behind that effort had also strengthened. The FCC approved an additional 7,500 Gen2 satellites for direct-to-cell operations outside the United States and supplemental coverage from space, giving SpaceX a larger authorized envelope than AST's own 248-satellite filing. That did not settle the question of service quality or country-by-country permissions, but it underscored the asymmetry in industrial scale between the two businesses. [FCC DA-26-36A1](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.pdf); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

AST's counter-position remained what its own filings and product pages said it was: larger arrays, a revenue model built around many carriers rather than one flagship U.S. carrier, and a constellation plan that management said could provide noncontinuous service in targeted markets with 25 total satellites, continuous coverage across key markets with 45 to 60 satellites, and continuous service across targeted geographies with about 90. In other words, the company was not arguing that it had launched faster than SpaceX. It was arguing that once scaled, its network architecture and commercial neutrality would matter more to operators than SpaceX's lead in first activation. [How it works](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/our-technology/); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

| | **AST SpaceMobile** | **Starlink / T-Satellite** |
|---|---|---|
| Operating model | Wholesale service through many MNOs | U.S. commercial launch through T-Mobile |
| Current disclosed partner footprint | Nearly 60 MNOs, more than 3 billion subscribers | T-Mobile launch; additional international expansion subject to separate carrier arrangements |
| Initial current-service threshold | 25 satellites for noncontinuous targeted markets; 45-60 for continuous key markets | Commercial text-led service launched July 2025 |
| Regulatory envelope cited in filings | 248-satellite AST network | 7,500 additional Gen2 D2C satellites approved by FCC in April 2026 |

| | **AST SpaceMobile** | **Starlink Direct to Cell** |
|---|---|---|
| Antenna aperture (operational) | Large phased array (~64 m²+ per satellite) | Integrated panel on v2 Mini bus (substantially smaller) |
| Spectrum model | Partner MNO's licensed terrestrial bands | SpaceX-licensed / T-Mobile Band 25 (US) |
| MNO partnerships | 50+ countries, AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, others | T-Mobile (US), bilateral international deals |
| Initial service tier | Voice, SMS, broadband data | SMS/text beta, voice and data follow-on |
| Operational milestone | BlueBird Block 1 launches Sep 2024 | Direct-to-Cell v2 Mini launches Jan 2024 |
| Ownership model | Independent listed company (NASDAQ: ASTS) | Division of privately held SpaceX |

The most structurally significant asymmetry may be financial. SpaceX's internal capital flows and lack of public-market disclosure obligations insulate Starlink Direct to Cell from the quarterly earnings scrutiny that AST faced as a listed company. SpaceX could cross-subsidise the Direct to Cell program from its broader Starlink broadband revenues. AST had no such backstop, which made the pace of its Block 2 satellite deployment and the conversion of its MNO agreements from letters of intent into revenue-generating commercial contracts the central financial narrative of its early operational years.

## Lynk Global: The Narrowband Incumbent

Lynk occupied a different position. Its own materials said it sent the first text message from space directly to a normal phone in March 2020, proved direct two-way connectivity in 2021, and received the first FCC license for commercial satellite-direct-to-standard-mobile-phone service in 2022. Lynk's public positioning leaned heavily toward emergency messaging, SMS and early roaming-style service rather than the higher-throughput broadband case AST emphasized. In that sense, Lynk mattered as both a competitor and a regulatory pathfinder. It showed that direct-to-device service could start with a text-led model and still be commercially relevant, even if AST's capacity ambitions were broader. [Lynk first text](https://lynk.world/news/lynk-sends-the-first-text-message-from-space-directly-to-a-normal-cell-phone/); [Lynk FCC license](https://lynk.world/news/fcc-grants-lynk-first-ever-license-for-commercial-satellite-direct-to-standard-mobile-phone-service/); [What We Do - Lynk](https://lynk.world/what-we-do/)

Lynk's commercial agreements concentrated on smaller and emerging-market carriers — operators in Africa, the Pacific Islands, and Southeast Asia for whom even basic text connectivity in rural dead zones was a meaningful service improvement. The architecture used much smaller satellites and accepted the throughput limitations that smaller apertures impose. For Lynk's target customers, this was sufficient: a carrier offering unmodified handset connectivity for emergency text or low-rate IoT telemetry did not need the broadband data rates that AST's large arrays were designed to deliver.

The competitive overlap with AST was therefore partial. Where AST pursued the major MNO relationships — AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Telstra, MTN — Lynk operated in segments those carriers had not prioritised. In practice, Lynk had arguably done more to validate the regulatory and commercial model than to compete directly for the same contracts. The existence of operational Lynk service, however modest in throughput, demonstrated to regulators in multiple jurisdictions that direct-to-cell satellite transmissions on terrestrial spectrum bands were technically and legally manageable — a proof of concept that eased some of the regulatory path for broader industry players.

## Apple and Globalstar: A Narrow-Band Reference Point

Apple's satellite feature was a different kind of competitive pressure. When Apple introduced the iPhone 14 in September 2022, it also introduced Emergency SOS via satellite, and in November 2022 it said the service had become available in the United States and Canada. Apple later said the feature had been made possible by a $450 million commitment to U.S. critical infrastructure, including Globalstar's network. This was not a broadband or general-purpose operator model. It was an emergency and location-sharing service tied to Apple hardware and tightly defined use cases. But it helped normalize the idea that an ordinary phone could reach a satellite in a moment of need, which indirectly worked in AST's favor even as it raised consumer awareness of a competing category of fallback connectivity. [iPhone 14 introduction](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2022/09/apple-introduces-iphone-14-and-iphone-14-plus/); [Emergency SOS availability](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2022/11/emergency-sos-via-satellite-available-today-on-the-iphone-14-lineup/); [Apple investment](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2022/11/emergency-sos-via-satellite-made-possible-by-450m-apple-investment/)

The service was explicitly limited: no voice, no broadband, emergency and location-reporting use cases only. It required antenna accommodation within Apple's own hardware, not generic handset compatibility. AST's entire proposition depended on connecting to any existing LTE-capable handset without modification — the billions of devices already in circulation globally. Apple-Globalstar demonstrated that the consumer market accepted satellite connectivity as a concept; it did not compete for the broadband and voice services that AST's architecture targeted.

## Where the Differentiation Line Holds

By May 2026 AST's defensible arguments were narrower than a simple "first and only" claim, but they were still real. The company could point to a large-antenna architecture already proven on BlueWalker 3 and BlueBird 1-5; a stated pathway from 25 to 45-to-60 to 90 satellites; a partner ecosystem broader than any single-carrier U.S. arrangement; and a 248-satellite network authorization that suggested a very large eventual footprint if capital and execution held. Against that, SpaceX could point to commercial launch, launch cadence, industrial scale and a deeper balance sheet; Lynk could point to early text-first proof and regulatory precedent; and Apple could point to mass consumer familiarity with satellite fallback. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

First, the antenna aperture advantage was physical and not easily replicated by competitors deploying smaller satellites at mass-production economics. Higher data rates per satellite required larger arrays, and larger arrays required either larger buses or unfurling mechanisms — both costly and logistically complex.

Second, the MNO partnership model provided a geographic and commercial reach that bilateral, carrier-by-carrier spectrum deals could not replicate at speed. By May 2026 AST was citing nearly 60 operator relationships covering more than 3 billion subscribers, giving it a broader declared commercial surface than any single-carrier U.S. arrangement. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

Third, the spectrum architecture — embedding AST infrastructure within the MNO's own licensed spectrum — created a legal and regulatory alignment with host-country carriers that an independent satellite operator deploying its own spectrum had to negotiate from a weaker position in most markets.

The competitive question had therefore shifted. It was no longer whether direct-to-cell would exist as a category. It was which version of the category would prove economically and operationally durable: a text-led safety layer, a carrier-specific commercial add-on, or a carrier-neutral broadband extension built around very large satellites and a long capital runway. That was the competitive frame in which AST entered the rest of 2026. [T-Mobile launch](https://www.t-mobile.com/news/network/best-network-in-america); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: From 2017 founding through BlueWalker, SPAC, BlueBird launches, MNO partnerships
chapters.body:
## The Founding Thesis

Abel Avellan incorporated AST SpaceMobile in Midland, Texas in 2017 carrying a proposition that the satellite communications establishment had largely dismissed as technically intractable: that a low Earth orbit constellation could connect directly to standard, unmodified smartphones without specialist hardware. The insight was not merely engineering — it was commercial. By routing service through existing mobile network operators rather than selling directly to consumers, AST could inherit subscriber bases numbering in the billions, bypass the subscriber-acquisition cost that had broken earlier satellite ventures, and access the licensed cellular spectrum that MNO partners already held. Avellan had sold his previous satellite communications company, Emerging Markets Communications, to Global Eagle Entertainment in 2016 for approximately $550 million, and brought that operational pedigree — alongside earlier stints at Hughes Electronics and Astrolink — to what would become the most consequential direct-to-cell bet in the capital markets.

The engineering challenge the founding thesis demanded was acute. Standard handsets transmit power in the range of one-quarter of a watt. Bridging that signal across the roughly 700-kilometre gap to a LEO satellite required an antenna aperture orders of magnitude larger than anything previously flown commercially — a large, unfurled phased-array that could concentrate enough gain to close the link. That antenna became the defining technical artifact of the BlueBird programme and the central uncertainty investors would price for years.

## SPAC Listing and Early Capital Formation

AST SpaceMobile went public on 7 April 2021 through a merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp, listing on Nasdaq under the ticker ASTS. The SPAC vehicle provided the balance-sheet capitalization needed to pursue a constellation program whose hardware costs, launch cadence and regulatory work were far beyond normal venture scale. The strategic capital timeline, however, was more staggered than some summaries suggested: Rakuten and Vodafone were the earlier lead investors; AT&T, Google and Vodafone then formed the January 2024 strategic package; Verizon added its own commitment in May 2024 through prepayments and notes rather than a simple equity check. [ASTS listing announcement](https://ast-science.com/2021/04/06/nasdaq-asts/); [Rakuten and Vodafone investment](https://ast-science.com/2020/03/03/rakuten-vodafone-invest-in-ast/); [January 2024 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224002914/form8-k.htm); [Verizon 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315224021726/form8-k.htm)

Revenue in the public period was modest, but the underlying pattern was not the simple engineering-services progression implied by the earlier draft. The 2022 10-K showed $13.8 million of revenue from the legacy NanoAvionika subsidiary. After AST sold its 51% stake in Nano in September 2022, 2023 revenue fell to zero. Revenue returned in 2024 at $4.4 million, largely from U.S. government milestones and gateway-equipment resale, before rising to $70.9 million in 2025 and $14.7 million in the first quarter of 2026. The financial profile remained capital intensive, but it was no longer accurate to describe 2022 through 2024 as a straight engineering-services revenue line. [2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017023011124/asts-20221231.htm); [2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024039342/asts-20231231.htm); [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm); [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

## BlueWalker 3: Proof of Concept in Orbit

The pivotal technical validation came on September 10, 2022, when AST SpaceMobile launched the BlueWalker 3 prototype aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral. BlueWalker 3 carried an unfurled phased-array antenna measuring approximately 693 square feet — the largest commercial communications antenna ever deployed in LEO at the time of launch. The satellite was not designed for commercial service; it was a demonstration platform to validate the link physics at scale and to generate the regulatory data needed for spectrum licensing globally.

Over the following months, the company reported a sequence of escalating test achievements. On 25 April 2023 it announced the first voice call from space to an ordinary smartphone. On 21 June 2023 it announced the first video call. On 19 September 2023 it announced what it described as the first 5G cellular broadband connection from space to an everyday smartphone, including a measured data rate of 14 Mbps. Those milestones reoriented investor perception of the program from speculative concept toward executable engineering. [first voice call](https://ast-science.com/2023/04/25/ast-spacemobile-makes-history-in-cellular-connectivity-completing-the-first-ever-space-based-voice-call-using-everyday-unmodified-smartphones/); [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/); [5G milestone](https://ast-science.com/ast-spacemobile-achieves-space-based-5g-cellular-broadband-connectivity-from-everyday-smartphones-another-historic-world-first/)

## BlueBird Block 1: First Operational Satellites

AST SpaceMobile launched its first five operational BlueBird satellites on 12 September 2024 aboard a Falcon 9. The launch marked the transition from prototype validation to commercial-grade hardware in orbit, but the hardware itself was less of a step change from BlueWalker 3 than the earlier draft implied. AST's own product pages described BlueBird 1-5 as using the same 693-square-foot class of phased array, with 40 MHz of bandwidth and peak speeds of 120 Mbps per coverage cell, while shifting the company from a single prototype to an initial commercial fleet. [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/)

The September 2024 deployment was followed by antenna deployment and early validation work rather than by an immediate consumer revenue inflection. AST later said it completed deployment of the communication phased-array antennas and Q/V antennas in October 2024. The 2024 10-K showed $4.4 million of revenue for the year, mainly from U.S. government milestones and gateway equipment resale, which underscored that the network had entered an early operational phase without yet reaching continuous mass-market service. [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm); [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/)

## MNO Partnership Architecture

The mobile-network-operator partnership roster that AST assembled between the 2021 listing and the frozen window constituted the commercial framework through which the direct-to-cell service would monetize. AT&T and Verizon anchored the United States; Vodafone, Rakuten, Bell Canada, Telstra, Orange, MTN and others extended the network internationally. By May 2026 AST was describing nearly 60 operator relationships covering more than 3 billion subscribers, a more precise and larger figure than the earlier shorthand around a fifty-country roster. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Partners](https://ast-science.com/company/mobile-network-operators/)

The commercial logic of the partnership model was that AST would charge MNOs on a wholesale basis for connectivity capacity consumed by their subscribers, while the MNOs handled the retail customer relationship, billing, and the regulatory spectrum licenses under which the service operated. Subscribers would receive service automatically when outside terrestrial coverage — no app download, no secondary SIM, no hardware change required. The simplicity of the customer experience was a deliberate design choice, intended to make the satellite layer effectively invisible and therefore scalable at the MNO's existing subscriber base without incremental marketing cost.

## Forward Catalysts at Frozen Snapshot

**Block 2 deployment.** Management said AST had reached planned manufacturing capacity for up to six Block 2 satellites per month and had fully assembled microns for up to 33 BlueBird satellites, but the commercial thresholds were still ahead: 25 total satellites for noncontinuous service in targeted markets, 45 to 60 for continuous coverage across key markets, and about 90 for continuous service across targeted geographies. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

**Commercial service conversion.** The first-quarter 2026 release paired the new FCC SCS authorization in the United States with nearly 60 operator relationships covering more than 3 billion subscribers. The next question was whether intermittent coverage and gateway deliveries would convert into sustained usage revenue once more satellites were in orbit. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

Additional operator additions still mattered, but by May 2026 the emphasis had shifted from logo collection to density and activation quality. Recent disclosures referenced Bell Canada, Telus, Orange, MTN, Vodacom and Axian Telecom, while 2025 year-end materials also pointed to expanded relationships with Telefonica, CK Hutchison, Taiwan Mobile and Sunrise. The question was no longer whether AST could persuade carriers to sign paper. It was whether the constellation could support enough coverage minutes to turn that paper into recurring usage. [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

Capital structure adequacy was the constraint threading through all three catalysts, but the status was again more specific than the earlier draft suggested. AST's March 2026 10-Q said management believed the company was fully funded for the costs necessary to manufacture and launch a constellation of approximately 90 satellites, while also warning that average capital cost could rise materially if cost reductions, supply-chain diversification and favorable launch contracts failed to materialize. That made capital adequacy a live risk, but not simply a blank placeholder for imminent dilution. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

## Key Dates

| Event | Date | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| BlueBird 6 launch | December 23, 2025 | First next-generation Block 2 satellite launched from India |
| BlueBird 7 loss | April 19, 2026 | New Glenn upper-stage anomaly led to deorbit and expected $155-$160 million write-off |
| U.S. SCS authorization | May 11, 2026 | AST said the FCC had authorized commercial SpaceMobile Service in the United States |
| Continuous-service threshold | Disclosed May 2026 | Management said about 45-60 total satellites were needed for continuous coverage across key markets |

chapters.title: Phased-array antenna, direct-to-cell engineering, and patent portfolio
chapters.body:
## The Aperture Problem and How Avellan Solved It

The engineering challenge at the heart of AST SpaceMobile's business is a physics problem that had defeated every previous attempt at satellite-to-handset connectivity: how to close a broadband communications link between a satellite 550 kilometres overhead and a smartphone designed to talk to a cell tower three kilometres away. The signal path is roughly two hundred times longer. The handset's antenna gain does not change. The satellite must compensate.

Every direct-to-cell predecessor accepted that constraint as a ceiling. The result was either narrowband messaging services or hardware-modified devices—approaches that required either truncated utility or MNO cooperation in distributing proprietary handsets. AST SpaceMobile's founders chose a third path: push the physics in the direction of aperture.

Abel Avellan and his chief scientist filed the company's first patent claims in 2017, the year they established the company in Midland, Texas. The foundational insight was that a sufficiently large phased-array antenna—deployed in low Earth orbit, driven by purpose-built digital signal processing—could generate enough effective isotropic radiated power to close a wideband 4G LTE link with a standard commercial handset. The phased array acts simultaneously as a spatially directed transmitter and a steerable receiver, electronically forming and moving beams across the coverage footprint without any mechanical articulation. The larger the aperture, the greater the antenna gain, and the more gain available to trade against the distance penalty of the orbital geometry.

## BlueWalker 3: Demonstrating the Principle at Scale

BlueWalker 3 made that engineering claim visible. AST said the satellite launched in September 2022 and completed deployment of its communications array in November 2022. The company described the array as 693 square feet and later used the satellite to announce the world's first voice call, video call and 5G connection from space to everyday smartphones. BlueWalker 3 therefore mattered not only as a prototype but as the first physical proof that AST's patents described something buildable and operable. [BlueWalker 3](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluewalker-3/); [first voice call](https://ast-science.com/2023/04/25/ast-spacemobile-makes-history-in-cellular-connectivity-completing-the-first-ever-space-based-voice-call-using-everyday-unmodified-smartphones/); [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/)

BlueWalker 3 later underpinned AST's April 2023 voice call, June 2023 video call and September 2023 5G announcement, moving the R&D story from deployable structure to live communications system. The same satellite also surfaced an unintended consequence: a Nature paper in 2023 found it was among the brightest objects in the night sky under some viewing conditions, forcing AST to treat reflectivity mitigation as part of later design work. [first voice call](https://ast-science.com/2023/04/25/ast-spacemobile-makes-history-in-cellular-connectivity-completing-the-first-ever-space-based-voice-call-using-everyday-unmodified-smartphones/); [Our Journey](https://ast-science.com/our-journey/); [Nature study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06672-7)

## The Doppler and Interference Problems

Operating in standard cellular bands from a platform moving at approximately 7.5 kilometres per second introduces two intertwined engineering problems that do not arise in geostationary satellite communications. At 2 GHz, orbital velocity produces a peak frequency offset of roughly ±50 kHz—beyond the tolerance of an unmodified LTE or 5G modem without correction. AST's approach, codified across its patent families and later aligned with 3GPP Release 17 and 18 NR-NTN specifications, places the Doppler pre-correction burden entirely on the satellite. The payload computes and applies a frequency offset that anticipates the shift each handset will experience, so that by the time the signal arrives at the phone, it falls within the modem's acceptable error window. The satellite's digital signal processor must execute this calculation continuously and independently for every simultaneous user beam.

The second constraint is terrestrial interference. AST SpaceMobile shares spectrum with its MNO partners—the same low-band and mid-band frequencies used by AT&T's 850 MHz network in the United States, Verizon's equivalent bands, and Vodafone's European allocations. A satellite beam with an uncontrolled footprint risks interfering with cell towers below in high-density areas. The company's beam-steering algorithms form tight spot beams so that each illuminates only the geographic zone where service is needed: where terrestrial coverage is dense, beams are withheld; where a user sits in a coverage gap, the beam is precisely directed. The patent literature describes configurations supporting hundreds of discrete simultaneous cells per satellite.

## The AST5000 ASIC: Proprietary Silicon as Structural Moat

AST said the AST5000 represented 150 person-years of R&D, had entered tape-out with TSMC in March 2024, and was intended to support 10 GHz of processing bandwidth. The company told investors that the chip would allow each next-generation BlueBird to support more than 2,000 active coverage cells and peak speeds of 120 Mbps per coverage cell. In other words, the silicon was not a marginal optimization. It was the bridge between a large antenna and a commercially useful network. [ASIC tape-out release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240327367837/en/AST-SpaceMobile-ASIC-Chip-Enters-Tape-Out-Phase-in-Collaboration-with-TSMC); [How it works](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/our-technology/)

Because the AST5000 is proprietary and radiation-hardened for the LEO environment, any competitor seeking to replicate the full system architecture would face a multi-year silicon development programme of comparable cost and duration before reaching production. This structural feature converts what might otherwise be a temporarily defensible engineering lead into a more durable barrier: ramping a novel ASIC from concept to production takes years even for well-capitalised organisations. Avellan has been direct about what this manufacturing achievement represents:

Management presented the AST5000 as evidence that AST was no longer only designing large antennas; it was also building the custom space-grade silicon needed to operate them at network scale. In that framing, the chip was not peripheral to the IP story. It was part of the moat. [ASIC tape-out release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240327367837/en/AST-SpaceMobile-ASIC-Chip-Enters-Tape-Out-Phase-in-Collaboration-with-TSMC); [How it works](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/our-technology/)

## The Patent Portfolio: Scope and Competitive Signal

AST publicly marked the 1,000th patent and patent-pending claim in March 2021. By December 2024 the company said the portfolio had grown past 3,500 claims with about 1,550 granted or allowed. By March 2026 those figures had increased again to about 3,900 total claims and about 2,000 granted or allowed. The board biography for Avellan also said he was an inventor on 24 U.S. patents, underscoring how closely the IP story remained tied to the founder personally. [1,000th claim announcement](https://ast-science.com/2021/03/12/ast-and-science-announces-1000th-patent-claim/); [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm); [Board bio](https://ast-science.com/investors/governance/board-of-directors/)

The most cited patent in the portfolio is [US9973266B1](https://patents.google.com/patent/US9973266B1/ko), "System and method for high throughput fractionated satellites (HTFS) for direct connectivity to and from end user devices and terminals using flight formations of small or very small satellites," which has received 96 forward citations from companies including Lynk Global and UbiquitiLink—direct competitors in the emerging direct-to-device sector. That citation pattern is diagnostic: the foundational architecture Avellan established has become the reference point against which later entrants must design around.

The substantive scope of those families mattered more than the headline count. AST said the portfolio covered large phased arrays, direct-to-cell architecture, high-power capability, deployment mechanisms, constellation management and satellite-to-phone connectivity techniques. Unlike consumer-software patent estates, which are often broad but operationally peripheral, AST's IP claims sat close to the company's manufacturing and service logic. The patents, the AST5000, and the manufacturing know-how were all describing the same defensible core. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm); [How it works](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/our-technology/)

## Block 2 and the Accumulating Aperture Advantage

The next-generation BlueBird program showed how AST was trying to compound that engineering lead. The public product page for the Block 2 fleet said the satellites carried arrays of nearly 2,400 square feet, roughly three times larger than the first-generation BlueBirds, and would deliver about 10 times the data capacity. BlueBird 6, launched in December 2025, became the first test of that architecture in orbit. The loss of BlueBird 7 in April 2026 was a setback, but it did not change the disclosed design target for the fleet that followed. [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

As of the frozen snapshot, AST's R&D and IP position therefore rested on three accumulated facts rather than on a generic innovation claim. First, it had flown and deployed the big array. Second, it had demonstrated voice, video and 5G links to everyday phones. Third, it had translated the underlying architecture into a production program with custom silicon, large manufacturing space and a still-expanding patent estate. Whether that would prove sufficient against better-capitalized competitors remained open. But by May 2026 it was no longer credible to treat AST's technology case as only conceptual. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

AST's own materials therefore kept returning to the same competitive claim in more measured form: the company viewed full direct-to-cell broadband to ordinary devices as a systems problem that demanded both aperture and processing scale, not just standards compliance. That was the intended consequence of combining the patent estate, the AST5000 ASIC and the larger next-generation BlueBird architecture. [How it works](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/our-technology/); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

Whether that exclusivity holds as 3GPP Release 18 and 19 NR-NTN standards make the underlying technical specifications more widely legible is one of the central questions in the sector. What the patent estate, the AST5000 ASIC, and the cumulative manufacturing learning curve collectively represent—as of the May 2026 snapshot—is a multi-year head start in a capital-intensive, physics-constrained discipline where catching up requires not just money but time.

chapters.title: Block 2 execution, Starlink competition, capital structure, regulatory
chapters.body:
## Block 2 Deployment Execution

The central execution risk no longer lay in proving that a single large satellite could talk to a phone. It lay in proving that AST could manufacture, test and launch enough next-generation satellites to turn intermittent service into continuous service. The company's March 2026 10-Q said it had completed planned investments to reach a production run-rate capacity of up to six Block 2 satellites per month, had fully assembled microns for up to 33 BlueBird satellites, and had supplier agreements and orders in place for the large majority of a planned constellation of more than 90 satellites. Those disclosures materially strengthened the manufacturing case relative to earlier years, but they did not remove schedule risk. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

Management itself listed the gating items: timely completion of assembly and testing, launch-vehicle readiness, logistics, regulatory approvals, launch windows and further capital where needed beyond the currently funded constellation size. The filing was also explicit that if AST could not achieve supply-chain diversification, cost reductions, process improvements and favorable launch contracts, the average capital cost of Block 2 satellites could be materially higher than planned. The risk, in other words, had moved from pure technology risk to industrial-execution risk. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

## Starlink Direct to Cell: Pressure From a Faster Scaler

Competitive pressure sharpened that execution risk. T-Mobile launched T-Satellite commercially in July 2025 with more than 657 Starlink direct-to-cell satellites already in orbit, while the FCC in April 2026 approved an additional 7,500 Gen2 satellites for direct-to-cell and supplemental-coverage uses. Whatever the differences in architecture or eventual throughput, SpaceX had already shown that it could move hardware into orbit at a pace AST had not yet matched. [T-Mobile launch](https://www.t-mobile.com/news/network/best-network-in-america); [FCC DA-26-36A1](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.pdf)

AST's counterclaim was that its coverage economics would improve materially once it reached its own constellation thresholds. But those thresholds - 25 satellites for noncontinuous service, 45 to 60 for continuous coverage across key markets, and about 90 for broader targeted geographies - were themselves dependent on the same manufacturing and launch cadence that competition made more urgent. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

## Capital Structure Adequacy Through the First Large Constellation

The liquidity story was better than in prior years, but not infinitely forgiving. AST said it had $3.4589 billion of cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash as of 31 March 2026 and believed it was fully funded for the costs necessary to manufacture and launch a constellation of about 90 satellites. That was a stronger statement than the company could make in 2023 or 2024. It also aligned with the backlog and prepayment disclosures around Verizon, stc and other operator contracts. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm); [stc 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315225020005/form8-k.htm)

But the same filing made clear that capital risk had not disappeared. The company still faced large launch payments, continued satellite manufacturing, and the possibility of higher-than-expected average capital costs. It also carried a much more complex convertible-debt structure than it had before 2025. A delay that might once have been absorbed with equity issuance now had to be assessed against multiple note issues, repurchase transactions and restricted-cash arrangements. [2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000006/asts-20251231.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

## Regulatory and Spectrum Coordination

AST's regulatory position also remained a mixed picture. The positive side was meaningful: the company said it had FCC authorization for commercial Supplemental Coverage from Space in the United States, authorization for its 248-satellite network, and a binding arrangement intended to secure long-term access to up to 45 MHz of lower mid-band spectrum in the United States and Canada through the Ligado transaction. Those were material advances over the earlier period when most of the regulatory story consisted of temporary authorities and forward-looking applications. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

The limiting side was equally clear: AST still needed additional approvals outside the United States before full commercial service could begin internationally, and it still depended on operating within partner carriers' terrestrial spectrum allocations country by country. The regulatory model was elegant, but it was also fragmented. It reduced AST's need to assemble a global spectrum position from scratch, yet it forced the company to clear many national gates instead of one. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

## Launch Risk After BlueBird 7

The loss of BlueBird 7 sharpened a risk that had always been present but had not yet become visible in the operating record. AST said the satellite was lost because New Glenn's upper stage placed it into too low an orbit to sustain operations, and estimated the carrying value at $155 million to $160 million. The company said it expected a replacement launch under its contract and had launch insurance covering part of the satellite and launch costs. Even so, the event was a reminder that constellation companies live at the intersection of their own execution and the reliability of third-party launch systems. [BlueBird 7 update](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315226018012/ex99-1.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

Taken together, the risk profile by May 2026 was more specific than it had been a year earlier. The company had already solved the first-order proof problem. What remained were the harder second-order ones: industrial scale, launch cadence, international permissions, cost discipline and competition from a rival already serving customers. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: Block 2 deployment, commercial revenue conversion, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Block 2 Inflection

By the time AST SpaceMobile's initial five BlueBird Block 1 satellites had completed their on-orbit commissioning in late 2024, Abel Avellan was already defining the next phase of the company's build-out in terms that left little room for ambiguity. Block 2 was not an incremental upgrade — it was the architecture that would make direct-to-cell economics work at scale.

The design distinction was fundamental, but by the frozen window AST had stopped describing it only in loose multiples. The company's public materials described the next-generation BlueBird satellites as carrying nearly 2,400 square feet of phased array, roughly three times the size of BlueBird 1-5 and about 10 times the data capacity. The March 2026 10-Q then translated that hardware claim into commercial thresholds: 25 total satellites for noncontinuous service in selected targeted markets, approximately 45 to 60 satellites for continuous coverage across key markets such as the United States, Europe and Japan, and roughly 90 satellites for continuous service across all targeted geographies. [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

AST's filings through the frozen window also showed a broader deployment path than the older Falcon-9-only framing implied. BlueBird 6 launched on ISRO's LVM3 in December 2025, BlueBird 7 launched on Blue Origin's New Glenn in April 2026 before being lost after the upper-stage anomaly, and management said it had reached planned production capacity of up to six next-generation satellites per month with fully assembled microns completed for up to 33 BlueBird satellites. The outlook was therefore tied not only to launch cadence, but to whether that manufacturing and launch stack could actually be sustained. [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/); [BlueBird 7 update](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000149315226018012/ex99-1.htm); [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

## MNO Revenue Conversion Mechanics

The structural logic of AST SpaceMobile's commercial model depended on a straightforward but operationally demanding sequence: launch satellites, achieve coverage, enable MNO partners to activate subscribers, and collect a revenue share. The partnership framework, as disclosed in commercial agreements with AT&T and Verizon in the United States, Vodafone across multiple European and African markets, and Rakuten in Japan, was built around wholesale arrangements in which the satellite operator would provide capacity to the MNO, with the carrier handling customer billing, plan packaging, and regulatory compliance in each jurisdiction.

AT&T's definitive agreement, Verizon's subsequent agreement, Vodafone's long-term framework and the broader international operator stack meant AST was not short of commercial counterparts by the frozen window. But the more relevant figure was the one management itself gave in May 2026: nearly 60 operator relationships covering more than 3 billion subscribers. That number clarified the bottleneck. The question was not whether AST could sign carriers; it was whether coverage would become continuous enough for those carriers to market the service in earnest. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

The revenue conversion challenge was not contractual but geometric. A single Block 1 satellite provided coverage over a given geographic footprint for only a fraction of each orbit, and five satellites could serve any given region for only minutes per day. Meaningful commercial revenue therefore required a constellation large enough to provide acceptable service continuity to paying subscribers. The reported revenue history underscored the transition: $13.8 million in 2022 from the legacy Nano subsidiary, zero in 2023 after the Nano sale, $4.4 million in 2024 from U.S. government milestones and gateway resale, $70.9 million in 2025, and $14.7 million in the first quarter of 2026. [2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017023011124/asts-20221231.htm); [2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017024039342/asts-20231231.htm); [2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm); [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000178031226000005/asts-ex99_1.htm); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

Block 2 deployment was therefore the linchpin of revenue conversion. Avellan, across multiple earnings call appearances through 2024, described the path to material commercial revenue as a function of constellation scale rather than any further contractual or technical uncertainty. The MNO partnerships were signed. The spectrum had been secured in most priority markets. The engineering proposition had been validated by BlueWalker 3 in 2022 and confirmed by Block 1 on-orbit operations in late 2024. What remained was putting enough satellites in orbit to generate the coverage minutes that would convert contracted agreements into cash receipts.

## Capital Structure and the 2025–2026 Funding Bridge

AST also gave a more confident funding answer than it had in earlier filings. The March 2026 10-Q said management believed the company was fully funded for the costs necessary to manufacture and launch a constellation of approximately 90 satellites. That statement rested on the enlarged 2025-2026 capital stack and on the $3.4589 billion of cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash disclosed at quarter-end. But it was still a bridge statement rather than an end-state one. The same filing warned that future average capital cost could rise materially if AST failed to secure cost reductions, process improvements and favorable launch contracts. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

The capital structure entering the Block 2 deployment phase carried meaningful dilution from the April 2021 SPAC merger and subsequent equity raises, but the investor base had consolidated around a set of strategic holders with long-duration interests in the commercial outcome. Vodafone, Rakuten, AT&T, and Google collectively held positions that aligned their incentives with execution rather than near-term financial exit. Convertible debt instruments introduced refinancing risk in the 2026–2027 window, a factor that sell-side analysts flagged as a potential source of additional dilution if constellation deployment timelines extended beyond guidance.

## Starlink Direct to Cell: The Competitive Constraint

The commercial clock was being set by competition as much as by AST's own roadmap. T-Satellite had already launched commercially in July 2025, and the FCC had expanded SpaceX's direct-to-cell authorization in April 2026. That did not mean Starlink and AST were strategically identical, but it did mean AST no longer had the luxury of scaling in a category with no active reference point. Every delay in reaching the 25-satellite and 45-to-60-satellite marks increased the probability that operators would compare AST not with the absence of service, but with an alternative already in market. [T-Mobile launch](https://www.t-mobile.com/news/network/best-network-in-america); [FCC DA-26-36A1](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.pdf)

The two architectures were not identical in their commercial positioning. Starlink's direct-to-cell service was built around a carrier-specific U.S. launch with T-Mobile first, while AST continued to argue for a carrier-neutral wholesale layer that could sit inside nearly 60 MNO relationships covering more than 3 billion subscribers. That difference did not erase SpaceX's head start, but it remained central to AST's claim that the company was building something broader than a one-carrier fallback feature. [T-Mobile launch](https://www.t-mobile.com/news/network/best-network-in-america); [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

Whether that differentiation proved commercially meaningful would ultimately depend on which architecture delivered superior coverage quality and subscriber economics at equivalent constellation sizes. The competitive pressure from Starlink DTC created urgency around Block 2 timeline execution. A prolonged deployment delay risked allowing T-Mobile to entrench an early-mover advantage with subscribers who — given the commodity nature of supplemental satellite coverage — might show limited inclination to switch providers once a service habit was established.

## 2026–2030: The Scaling Horizon

The most useful way to think about the outlook, as of the frozen window, was therefore through the milestones management itself had disclosed rather than through old external model assumptions.

| Milestone | Management's disclosed scale | Commercial significance |
|---|---|---|
| Initial targeted-market service | 25 total BlueBird satellites | Noncontinuous service in selected targeted markets |
| Continuous key-market coverage | Approximately 45-60 satellites | Continuous service across the United States, Europe, Japan and other strategic markets |
| Continuous targeted-geography coverage | Approximately 90 satellites | Continuous service across all targeted geographies tied to long-term business goals |
| Longer-term network envelope | 248 satellites authorized by FCC | Broader capacity and geographic expansion beyond the initial funded constellation |

The company's own guidance therefore implied a multi-stage build rather than a single global flip of the switch. The first stage was getting enough satellites up to make the service commercially real. The second was using that proof to turn signed operators into recurring traffic. The third was using the early network to justify the capital and regulatory effort behind the larger 248-satellite envelope. That was the outlook AST had actually disclosed by 23 May 2026. [Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216950/asts-20260331.htm)

For Avellan, who had founded the company in Midland, Texas in 2017 with the explicit thesis that existing unmodified smartphones were already radio-compatible with a sufficiently large low-orbit phased array, the 2026–2030 horizon was not speculative territory. It was the execution phase of an engineering proposition that BlueWalker 3 had validated in September 2022 and Block 1 had confirmed in the autumn of 2024. Whether the commercial build-out could proceed at the pace the capital structure required — and far enough ahead of a Starlink Direct to Cell competitor with substantially deeper resources — remained the central, unresolved question facing the company at the frozen snapshot date.

## C. Technology Glossary

**BlueWalker 3** - AST's prototype direct-to-cell satellite, launched in September 2022 with a 693-square-foot phased array. [BlueWalker 3](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluewalker-3/)

**BlueBird 1-5** - The first five commercial satellites, launched in September 2024, each with a 693-square-foot phased array. [BlueBird 1-5](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/bluebird-1-5/)

**Next-generation BlueBird** - The larger Block 2 design, described by AST as carrying nearly 2,400 square feet of phased array and about 10 times the data capacity of Block 1. [Next-Generation BlueBird](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/next-gen-bluebird/)

**AST5000** - AST's custom application-specific integrated circuit designed to support 10 GHz of processing bandwidth and more than 2,000 coverage cells per satellite. [How it works](https://ast-science.com/spacemobile-network/our-technology/)

**SCS** - Supplemental Coverage from Space, the FCC framework under which AST said it obtained U.S. commercial authorization in May 2026. [Q1 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000119312526216946/asts-ex99_1.htm)

financials.key_finding: AST SpaceMobile is pre-commercial-revenue. The April 2021 SPAC merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp listed the company on NASDAQ. The September 2024 BlueBird Block 1 launches (first 5 operational satellites) transitioned the company from pre-operational to early operational. The MNO partnership commercial revenue conversion plus the Block 2 deployment scaling are the principal forward strategic events.
structural_observations: Revenue is principally engineering services and pre-commercial partner contributions; commercial mobile service revenue has not begun materially.
Substantial operating losses reflecting pre-commercial constellation build-out.
Capital raises: post-SPAC equity plus subsequent equity and convertible debt instruments to fund constellation deployment.
Strategic equity partners include Vodafone, Rakuten, AT&T, Google — substantial pre-commercial validation.
BlueBird Block 1 (first 5 satellites launched September 12 2024 via SpaceX Falcon 9) demonstrated commercial-grade direct-to-cell capability.
Block 2 satellite design is substantially larger (~2-3x antenna area) targeting higher capacity per satellite; deployment scaling through 2025-2026.

leadership.key_finding: AST SpaceMobile is structurally founder Abel Avellan's company. Avellan serves as Chairman of the Board, Chief Executive Officer, and President — a triple-role structure that signals concentrated founder operational control through the multi-year capital-intensive constellation deployment programme. CFO Andrew Johnson and Chief Strategy Officer Sean Wallace plus the broader executive team support Avellan's leadership. The board includes representatives from major strategic investors (AT&T, Rakuten, Vodafone, Verizon plus the SPAC-era directors) reflecting the company's strategic partnership architecture with the major global mobile network operators.

ceo_chairman_president.framing: Avellan founded AST SpaceMobile in 2017 with the founding thesis that direct-to-cell satellite connectivity could become a meaningful commercial service through a low Earth orbit constellation designed to provide cellular broadband directly to standard unmodified mobile phones. The Venezuelan-born telecommunications industry veteran brought multi-decade satellite communications operational experience including the previous successful entrepreneurship at EMC (which sold to Global Eagle Entertainment in 2016) plus broader Hughes Electronics and Astrolink pedigree. The triple-role structure (Chairman + CEO + President) signals concentrated founder control; the continued continuity from founding through the 2021 SPAC listing and into the post-public period has been the structural anchor of the company's strategic direction. Avellan's substantial equity ownership plus the institutional shareholder structure (with strategic mobile network operator equity participation) supports continued operational and governance leadership through the multi-year deployment programme.

leadership.board_composition_observation: AST SpaceMobile's board pairs founder Chairman/CEO/President Abel Avellan with directors representing the major strategic mobile network operator investors (AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten) plus additional independent directors. The composition reflects the company's strategic partnership architecture — the direct-to-cell service depends on mobile network operator partnerships for both the spectrum access (the MNO partners provide the cellular spectrum the satellites use to provide service to MNO customers) and the customer monetisation. The MNO board representation aligns governance with these strategic relationships and provides ongoing communication channels at the senior level. The forward governance trajectory through the constellation deployment and commercial scaling depends on continued Avellan operational leadership plus the broader board composition's support of the multi-year strategic execution.
